items.title: Like a 'vertical roller coaster': Simulating flydubai flight FZ1073's sudden plunge
items.description: Flydubai’s flight FZ1073, which plunged 16,000 feet in about 30 seconds before being levelled out and landing safely, would have felt like a “vertical roller coaster”, according to an aviation instructor who recreated the descent in a flight simulator for Reuters . The steep fall, after an attack on the captain by the co-pilot during a flight on Wednesday, would have put huge strain on the Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft — as well as the passengers and crew, said Alberto Paduanelli, owner of ALPA Simulation in Sherfield on Loddon, southern England. The co-pilot of the flydubai jet, which was bound for Israel from Dubai, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, calling the incident a “ terrorist attack ”. The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, two sources with knowledge of the investigation told Reuters . UAE authorities did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation of his identity. Reuters could not independently reach al-Hammami for comment. Flydubai says the circumstances surrounding the incident are still under investigation and it cannot comment further. Oman has yet to comment on the incident. “A plunge of 16,000 feet (4,877 metres) over 30 seconds will feel like you are over on a very, very vertical roller coaster,” Paduanelli said, sitting at the controls of the simulator cockpit. “The difference is that on the roller coaster, you know what’s happening,” he said, adding that with a sudden drop “you feel the negative g-force on your body”. For passengers who are not strapped in, “Your body will literally lift from the seat”, he said. Using a simulator to recreate the incident, Paduanelli said the aircraft’s autopilot disconnected before the plunge began, causing the jet to accelerate rapidly. United States President Donald Trump has praised the Boeing jet for withstanding the severe forces put on it during the incident. The plane was levelled out after passengers overpowered the co-pilot, before a reserve crew of pilots onboard landed the plane. “It was an amazing show of precise and powerful structural planning and design,” Trump posted on Truth Social, adding that the 737 MAX “was able to withstand G Forces and Strain far beyond what it was designed and expected to do”. Boeing did not respond to a request for comment. Aircraft are designed and tested to withstand substantial aerodynamic loads, but Paduanelli said a prolonged high-speed dive can place extreme strain on an airframe. “This was nothing but a miracle that nothing was hurt apart from the captain, unfortunately, and that two pilots were onboard,” Paduanelli said. Details about al-Hammami’s past have trickled out. Royal Air Maroc told Reuters he did a three-month training with the airline in 2025 but his application to work there afterwards was rejected. Buckinghamshire New University in Britain said he did a distance-learning course in aviation management with the institution, but no pilot training. An Australian Federal Police spokesperson said on Sunday that authorities there were investigating al-Hammami’s “links to Australia”. A source briefed on the investigation said the co-pilot studied at a university in Melbourne.

items.title: Grand Prix de Bahreïn : Verstappen domine une course retardée par la mousson
items.description: Le quadruple champion du monde Max Verstappen (Red Bull) a remporté dimanche le Grand Prix de Bahreïn délocalisé en Malaisie, au terme d'une course retardée d'une heure et demie en raison d'une forte pluie de mousson avant le départ. Le Néerlandais, qui a brillé tout le week-end, gagne ainsi sa première victoire de la saison, devançant le jeune leader du championnat du monde Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) et le septuple champion du monde britannique Lewis Hamilton en Ferrari. Le coéquipier de ce dernier, le Monégasque Charles Leclerc, est quatrième et le Français Isack Hadjar en Red Bull complète ce top 5. Les Mercedes d'Antonelli et du Britannique George Russell, ont ainsi viré en tête au premier virage en dépassant Verstappen parti en pole position et Hamilton qui était deuxième sur la ligne de départ. Verstappen a ensuite repris les commandes et a maîtrisé les 55 tours de 5,543 km chacun. items.title: Agoè-Nyivé /110 élèves démunis bénéficient de tenues et de kits scolaires
items.description: Agoè-Nyivé, 4 oct. (ATOP) – Cent dix élèves démunis des communes Agoè-Nyivé 3 et 6 ont bénéficié de tenues et de kits scolaires, le vendredi 2 octobre au centre communautaire de la commune d’Agoè-Nyivé 3. Les kits scolaires remis aux bénéficiaires sont composés notamment de tenues scolaires, de cahiers de 200 et de 100 pages, d’ensembles géométriques, de paquets de crayons de couleur, de règles et d’ardoises. Ce don est à l’initiative de l’Association des couturières et tailleurs de Vakpossito (ACTAV), en collaboration avec le Conglomérat Horizon 2000 et la mairie d’Agoè-Nyivé 3. L’adjoint au maire remet un kit à une bénéficiaire Dans la commune Agoè-Nyivé 3, l’ACTAV a pris en charge 95 élèves issus de trois établissements scolaires, à savoir l’EPP Vakpossito, l’EPP Elavagnon et l’EPP Logogomé, pour un coût total de 385.000 F CFA. Chaque bénéficiaire a reçu une tenue scolaire, deux cahiers de 200 pages, quatre cahiers de 100 pages, un ensemble géométrique, un paquet de crayons de couleur, une règle et une ardoise. Dans la commune d’Agoè-Nyivé 6, quinze (15) élèves démunis ont aussi bénéficié des mêmes kits scolaires. Le maire adjoint de la commune Agoè-Nyivé 3, Alidjinou Mitognawo Eli, a relevé que cette action traduit une volonté commune de faire de l’éducation une priorité et de contribuer à offrir aux enfants les conditions nécessaires pour apprendre, grandir et construire leur avenir. Il a salué l’initiative de l’ACTAV en faveur des enfants démunis et exprimé sa reconnaissance au Conglomérat Horizon 2000, qui a également apporté son soutien en distribuant des kits scolaires à une vingtaine d’élèves. Le président de l’organisation, conseiller de l’ACTAV, Ahondo Georges a expliqué que cette initiative est née d’une réflexion suscitée par les travaux de retouche d’habits effectués pour certains élèves. « En constatant les difficultés vestimentaires de certains enfants, nous avons pensé qu’il était nécessaire d’agir pour leur apporter notre soutien », a-t-il expliqué. Dans cette démarche, les membres de l’association se sont rendus dans les établissements scolaires concernés afin d’identifier les besoins des élèves et prendre leurs mesures sur place pour confectionner à chacun une tenue scolaire adaptée. Bayamina Marie-José, élève en classe de CM1 et bénéficiaire du don, a exprimé sa gratitude aux donateurs pour ce geste qui vient soulager les difficultés auxquelles ils sont confrontés. Elle a promis de redoubler d’efforts afin de réussir son année scolaire. Cette action de solidarité s’inscrit dans la dynamique d’accompagnement des enfants démunis et de promotion de l’accès à l’éducation, particulièrement en cette période de rentrée scolaire. La cérémonie de remise s’est déroulée, en présence des parents d’élèves, des directeurs d’établissements scolaires, ainsi que des tailleurs et couturières de la commune. ATOP/ASA/SED/KYA

items.title: France: la police accusée de réprimer les jeunes, le ministre de l'Intérieur réfute
items.description: Les forces de l'ordre « ne répriment pas la jeunesse » mais « protègent » élèves et étudiants désireux de « porter pacifiquement leurs revendications », a assuré dimanche le ministre de l'Intérieur Laurent Nuñez, alors que les accusations de d'usage disproportionné de la force se multiplient. Policiers et gendarmes « interviennent avec fermeté et sans délai pour faire cesser les dégradations, violences, exactions commises par les fauteurs de troubles et ce avec proportionnalité sous le contrôle de leur hiérarchie et le cas échéant de la Justice », a souligné le ministre de l'Intérieur sur son compte X. Répondant au syndicat de la magistrature (SM), qui a appelé à cesser « de réprimer la jeunesse pour la faire taire », Laurent Nuñez a déploré des « accusations graves et sans fondement d'interventions soi-disant brutales et disproportionnées qui seraient dirigées de surcroît contre +les jeunes racisés issus des quartiers populaires+ ». Il a également regretté une « communication accusatoire totalement déconnectée du monde réel » de la part du syndicat. Dans un télégramme diffusé sur X mercredi, le ministre français de l'Intérieur, avait appelé les forces de l'ordre au « discernement », avec « un usage de la force strictement proportionné » en rappelant qu'une « grande majorité des personnes interpellées sont des mineurs ». Des vidéos circulant sur les réseaux sociaux, notamment de médias français, montrent des interventions très musclées des forces de l'ordre face à des mineurs, ayant provoqué la colère et la consternation des internautes. Dans le ville de Tours, mercredi, un jeune homme âgé de 16 ans a perdu l’usage de son œil droit après un tir de LBD, selon le média 20minutes. Des membres du corps enseignant et des maries dans plusieurs villes du pays se sont joints aux manifestations des étudiants pour les soutenir dans leurs revendications. C'était le cas notamment à Nanterre devant devant le lycée Joliot-Curie où une manifestation immobile devait avoir lieu. « De nombreux adultes ont formé un cordon pour protéger les jeunes », indique 20minutes, en ajoutant que selon les personnels de l’établissement, les forces de l’ordre ont avancé «sans sommation ni aucune forme de communication ». Dans un communiqué daté du 2 octobre, ils dénoncent des interventions « disproportionnées » et parlent de « violences policières », des lanceurs de balles de défense « directement pointés vers les élèves et les adultes présents ». Ils décrivent une ligne de policiers équipés de matraques télescopiques, de boucliers et de lanceurs de balles de défense face aux adolescents qui étaient immobiles. Un élu de la mairie aurait été « matraqué à plusieurs reprises » selon le communiqué, tandis qu'un policier aurait posé l’avant-bras sur la gorge d’un enseignant pour le faire reculer. Les personnels font aussi état d’insultes et de menaces, comme « c’est toi que je vais taper » ou encore « bande de salopes », toujours selon la même source. Depuis lundi, les autorités françaises ont dénombré plus de 5.000 interpellations, dont environ 85% de mineurs, en marge du mouvement de blocage lycéen. Pour la seule journée de vendredi, marquée par des tensions avec les forces de l'ordre, il y a eu plus de 1.700 interpellations lors de cette mobilisation pour réclamer davantage de moyens, plus d'enseignants et dénoncer l'interdiction des téléphones portables dans les établissements. Selon les chiffres de jeudi soir cités par le ministre Edouard Geffray sur France 2, au moins 170 jeunes ont été blessés et 65 membres du personnel ont subi des blessures depuis le début du mouvement. L'inspection générale de la police nationale (IGPN), la « police des polices », a été saisie de cinq enquêtes, après que des lycéens ont été blessés par des tirs de lanceurs de balles de défense (LBD) et de grenades, a indiqué vendredi France Télévisions de source sécuritaire. The post France: la police accusée de réprimer les jeunes, le ministre de l'Intérieur réfute appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Amb. Edward Boateng congratulates Boadu, Kodua on election wins
items.description: Former Ghanaian Ambassador to China, Edward Boateng, has congratulated John Boadu and Justin Frimpong Kodua on their election and re-election, respectively, as National Chairman and General Secretary of the New Patriotic Party (NPP). Mr Boateng said the results of the NPP’s National Delegates Conference come with a significant responsibility for both leaders to rebuild the party, strengthen its structures and unite its members ahead of the 2028 general elections. Congratulating Mr Boadu, he said his extensive experience within the NPP places him in a position to lead efforts to reorganise the party from the grassroots to the national level. “Chairman John Boadu’s remarkable journey—from the polling station and constituency levels through National Youth Organiser, National Organiser, Acting General Secretary and General Secretary to National Chairman—is a testament to his dedication, sacrifice and commitment to our Party,” he said. Mr Boateng had, prior to the October 3 election, publicly endorsed Mr Boadu’s candidacy, saying he had worked with all the candidates and had carefully considered their respective experience and leadership qualities. He said Mr Boadu’s experience, institutional knowledge, temperament and willingness to listen made him the candidate he believed was suited to lead the party at the time. Mr Boateng also highlighted Mr Boadu’s previous service as National Organiser and Acting General Secretary between 2014 and 2016, saying he helped rebuild the NPP’s organisational machinery and contributed to the party’s 2016 electoral victory. He has now urged the new National Chairman to use his mandate to promote reconciliation within the party and bring together members who supported different candidates during the internal elections. “Every tradition and tendency within the NPP must find a place in the rebuilding effort,” he said. Turning to Mr Kodua, Mr Boateng congratulated him on retaining the General Secretary position, describing his victory as an expression of the confidence delegates have placed in him. He also noted that Mr Kodua had entered the history of the NPP by becoming the first person since Dan Botwe to win election as General Secretary for a second consecutive term. Mr Boateng said Mr Kodua must now work closely with Chairman Boadu to reorganise and strengthen the party’s structures and ensure they function effectively from the polling station to the national level. “With such an emphatic mandate comes an equally significant responsibility,” he said. He urged the General Secretary to lead with competence, fairness and humility, while strengthening discipline and accountability and remaining accessible to the grassroots. Mr Boateng further called on Mr Kodua to reach out to members who supported other candidates and help heal divisions that may have emerged during the internal elections. He said the Chairman and General Secretary must work with the entire national leadership to build a strong and united political organisation capable of supporting the NPP’s Flagbearer, Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, ahead of the 2028 general elections. The NPP’s National Delegates Conference was held at the Baba Yara Sports Stadium in Kumasi on Saturday, October 3. Mr Boadu was elected National Chairman with 2,888 votes, defeating Boakye Kyerematen Agyarko, who polled 2,408 votes. Former National Chairman Paul Afoko received 790 votes, while Sammy Crabbe obtained 41 votes. Mr Kodua retained the General Secretary position with 4,486 votes. Mr Boateng said the new leadership must use the mandate given to them to rebuild a disciplined, united and formidable NPP capable of restoring public confidence in the party.

items.title: Assoli /Jubilé de diamant : Le CEG de Bafilo-ville célèbre son soixantenaire
items.description: Bafilo, 4 oct. (ATOP) – Le Collège d’enseignement général (CEG) de Bafilo-ville a célébré ses 60 années d’existence, le samedi 3 octobre à Bafilo. La cérémonie a été couplée d’une remise de 2 salles de classes équipées de 60 tables bancs. L’organisation est à l’actif de l’association des Anciens élèves et enseignants du CEG Bafilo-ville (AECEBA) qui, par ses cotisations propres, a construit une bâtisse de 2 salles de classes pour leur ancien établissement. Le coût de la construction de cette bâtisse est évalué à 5 874 200 FCFA et l’équipement de tables bancs à 794 000 FCFA. Ce don n’est pas le premier geste de l’association. Les autorités L’historique du CEG revèle que dans les années antérieures, AECEBA a lutté contre COVID-19 en offrant à cet établissement notamment, un lot de matériel de santé, des tables bancs, d’un kit complet de matériel de laboratoire et de manuels scolaires importés de France. La célébration a consisté à une coupure du ruban par le préfet d’Assoli, Lt-Col Viagbo Mensah et une visite des autorités dans les salles de classes de ladite bâtisse. Le président de l’AECEBA, Akakpo Ikpadon a rendu hommage aux anciens directeurs, enseignants et élèves du Collège aujourd’hui disparus. Il a signifié que leur association est à caractère apolitique, représentée comme le Togo en miniature, réunissant plusieurs ethnies autour d’objectifs communs. Il a invité toute bonne volonté à soutenir l’action de l’association pour la réalisation de l’ensemble de ses projets. La bâtisse offerte Le représentant du pouvoir central, Lt-col Viagbo a exprimé sa gratitude à l’association pour la construction du bâtiment qui répond, dit-il, aux besoins du gouvernement. Cette réalisation, ajoute-t-il, est un investissement durable au profit des apprenants qui doivent en prendre soin. Il a exhorté les bénéficiaires à l’assiduité et au corps enseignant à un bon encadrement. « Nous célébrons le passé de l’école, mais pensons aussi à son avenir », a-t-il martelé. Cette célébration du jubilé de diamant a connu la présence des autorités notamment, les responsables de l’éducation régionale de la Kara, les maires des 3 communes d’Assoli, les responsables administratifs et sécuritaires de la préfecture. ATOP/GMM/SED/KYA

John Boadu pledges to rebuild NPP from grassroots and restore ‘winning machinery’
items.description: Newly elected National Chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), John Boadu, has pledged to rebuild the party from the grassroots and restore its “winning machinery” following his election at the party’s National Delegates Conference in Kumasi. Mr Boadu secured 2,888 votes to defeat his closest contender, Boakye Kyerematen Agyarko, who polled 2,408 votes. Delivering his acceptance speech after the results were declared, Mr Boadu said his election represented a responsibility to serve the party rather than a personal victory. “Today is not merely a day of victory. It is a day of responsibility and of great unity. I stand before you with a heart full of gratitude and humility,” he said. Mr Boadu extended a hand of friendship to the candidates who contested the chairmanship race, saying their experience and ideas remained valuable to the NPP. “To those who contested with us, I extend my hand of friendship and partnership. Your ideas, experience, networks and commitments belong to the New Patriotic Party,” he said. He rejected the idea of a divided party following the contest. “There must be no winners and losers. Only one NPP united around one purpose,” he declared. Mr Boadu said the party must learn, adapt and become more responsive to the changing expectations of Ghanaians. “Our task is to build a renewed NPP, one that listens more, consults more, organises better, and prepares more deliberately for the future,” he said. He pledged to work with regional and constituency executives, Members of Parliament, the Minority Caucus, party patrons, external branches and other groups within the party. The newly elected Chairman placed young people at the centre of his agenda, saying they must feel a sense of belonging within the NPP. “Our young people must feel that the NPP is their home,” he said. He also promised to deepen the party’s engagement with TESCON, voluntary groups, social media practitioners and the traditional media. “A modern political organisation must engage every means of communicating responsibility,” he stated. He further proposed developing tertiary institutions as centres for constructive political dialogue and leadership development. Mr Boadu said the new executive team would work with the party’s flagbearer, Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, to strengthen the NPP’s organisational and financial structures, particularly at the constituency level. He cautioned that electoral success could not be taken for granted. “Political victory is never an entitlement. It must be earned through service, organisation, credibility, and the trust of the Ghanaian people. That is why our preparation begins now,” he said. Mr Boadu called on members to put the collective interest of the party ahead of individual ambitions. “Let us choose unity over division, service over personal ambition, organisation over disorder, and hope over despair,” he urged. He also pledged that his executive team would lead through consultation and work with all sections of the party. “We will serve the New Patriotic Party with humility, lead through consultation, work with every part of our party, and dedicate this mandate to restoring the winning machinery of our great party,” he said. He concluded with a declaration of confidence in the party’s prospects in the next general election. “JB and his executives are back again. Victory is assured in the year 2028,” he stated. Mr Boadu’s election marks a return to the NPP’s national executive leadership after he lost the General Secretary contest to Justin Frimpong Kodua at the party’s 2022 National Delegates Conference. Mr Kodua retained the General Secretary position in the latest election. The new leadership takes charge as the NPP seeks to reorganise its structures following its defeat in the 2024 general election and prepare for the 2028 contest. Mr Boadu’s challenge will now be to translate his pledges on grassroots mobilisation, unity and organisational renewal into the party’s operations over the next four years.

items.title: La Policía empieza a desalojar el asentamiento de migrantes de la playa de El Trampolín de Ceuta
items.description: La Policía Nacional ha empezado a desalojar de manera parcial el asentamiento de migrantes de la playa de El Trampolín , en Ceuta, con un operativo de gran envergadura desarrollado este domingo. La primera furgoneta de la Unidad de Intervención Nacional (UIP) ha llegado sobre las 7.30, cuando aún no había amanecido y la bruma cubría el mar, para una primera toma de contacto. Minutos después, un dron ha empezado a sobrevolar la zona. Finalmente, ya a las 8.00 y por sorpresa, medio centenar de furgonetas de la Policía Nacional, tres tanquetas de los antidisturbios y otra decena de vehículos pesados del Ejército han irrumpido entre la neblina, todos de golpe, para arrancar el dispositivo. items.title: A Reckoning in Springfield
items.description: Photographs by Carol Guzy H e kept going over the details. “I run this route every day, like clockwork,” the trucker was saying, heading west to where he had first seen the man on the side of the highway. Now it was a Sunday morning, his day off, and Jack Buhring was driving his mother’s minivan, retracing the route, trying to make sense of what had happened less than a week before. His girlfriend, Renee Claytor, was in the passenger seat, studying him, then looking out the window. His mother, Diana Buhring, was in the back. “It wasn’t your fault,” she kept saying, and “Jack, do you think you’re still in shock?” But her son was not really listening. “Mondays—that’s usually my long day,” he continued. Up at 1:30 a.m., shower, coffee, and by 2 a.m. he’d be pulling out of the mobile-home park in Chillicothe, the southern-Ohio town where he had grown up, gotten his first job hauling garbage, his second job driving cross-country, and the one he had now, hauling powdered concrete hardener in a Kenworth T800. Fairborn to Westerville, Westerville to Fairborn, repeat. Two loops, paid per load, no health insurance, and a recliner where he fell asleep most evenings. Those were the basics of Jack Buhring’s 41-year-old life, and just after eight that Monday morning, August 31, he had reached his favorite part of the route, a westbound stretch of highway running through miles of cornfields and wildflowers near Springfield, a small city that he passed each day, and whose recent troubles had barely registered as a series of memes and headlines that he’d mostly tried to avoid. “We’re getting closer,” he said now, passing the fields. “We’re coming up on it.” He’d been in the right lane, he said, when he’d noticed a car rolling to a stop on the right shoulder. As he flipped on his left turn signal to move out of the way, he’d seen a man getting out of the car, who was then walking toward his trunk, who was then continuing on against traffic, then running—then diving out in front of him. [ Read: The northern passage ] “Right here,” Jack said as he drove over black tire marks curving left across all three lanes. “See, I locked it down right here. You can see where I swerved. See? I started to signal and—it just happened so fast.” Renee and Diana glanced back at the marks. Jack continued: An SUV and another truck behind him had swerved to a stop. The other trucker had helped Jack out of the cab, which had somehow been jammed shut, and checked on the man, who had been caught under Jack’s truck. Jack, who was not physically injured, had called 911 and told the dispatcher that a man had jumped in front of him, and—“Oh my God. I killed him.” Waiting on state troopers, he had looked around and seen a black device about 20 feet from his truck. He realized that it was an ankle monitor, smashed and blinking red. “I started trying to put two and two together,” he said now, continuing west on the highway. “I said, ‘I hope he’s not a troubled kid, down on his luck, in trouble with the cops.’ That’s the first thing that come through my mind.” Then the state troopers had arrived, and after a while, one of them told Jack that it was a young Haitian man from Springfield. At that point, Jack didn’t understand the full significance of what the trooper had said. He was shaking and sweating in the middle of the highway. He called his boss to tell him what had happened. He sat in a trooper’s car and gave his report. He cleared a drug test. Then he started asking questions that the troopers could not immediately answer. He wanted to know the young man’s name. He wanted to know if he had kids. He wanted to know anything about him. Carol Guzy A truck on I-70 in Ohio passes mile marker 66, where Pierre Damas Bel died when he walked into traffic. W hen he got home later that afternoon, Renee told Jack what she was hearing on the news, a story that would soon become another defining moment in the Trump administration’s mass-deportation campaign. More and more, Americans going about their regular lives were witnessing black SUVs roaming parking lots and gas stations, neighbors and colleagues disappearing, and sometimes ICE agents grabbing, tackling, or even shooting people, forcing a thousand quiet reckonings with what the country has become. This time the violence was being investigated as a suicide, the witness was Jack, and the reckoning began as Renee told him the young man’s name, Pierre Damas Bel. He was 20, and had arrived legally in the United States in March 2024 and been granted something called Temporary Protective Status, or TPS, due to dangerous conditions in Haiti. He had joined his family in Springfield, where roughly 15,000 Haitians had settled in recent years. He had just graduated from high school, where he’d been a standout student, soccer player, and member of the Junior ROTC program. He’d enrolled at Wright State University, half an hour from Springfield, and wanted to study neuroscience. The news coverage mentioned that the Trump administration had revoked TPS for approximately 350,000 Haitian nationals living in the U.S., which Jack remembered hearing something about. And that in recent weeks, ICE had started ordering Haitians in Springfield to check in at field offices, where they were being fitted with ankle monitors, which Jack had not known about. By the next day, he’d heard that Bel’s father, Ronal Bel, who declined to be interviewed for this story, had put out a statement saying that “after my son was outfitted with this ankle monitor, he felt like he was treated like an animal.” Ronal wrote that his son had told him that classmates had bullied him because of the ankle monitor and that he felt “humiliated,” and that he’d called moments before his death to tell his father that he was not “feeling okay.” Jack heard that politicians and activists, including a Springfield pastor named Carl Ruby, were blaming the Trump administration for what happened. “It’s our immigration policy that took his life,” Ruby had told reporters. Jack thought about that. He was a lifelong Democrat who had voted for Trump for the first time in 2024, reasoning that things weren’t getting better, so why not try something different. He’d supported what Trump had said about deporting undocumented immigrants convicted of crimes, but none of what he was learning now sounded like that. Carol Guzy Carl Ruby, the pastor at Central Christian Church in Springfield, comforts Ronal Bel on the day that his son died. He began searching for more details about the young man he was now calling Pierre. He found his social-media pages. Here was Pierre in a blue suit receiving an award from a local business group. Here he was smiling in his JROTC uniform. Here he was at an award ceremony for Texas Roadhouse, where he’d worked as a waiter, and playing on a soccer field. And here was the photo of Pierre’s left leg, the bulky black monitor clamped around his ankle, the red light glowing above a shiny black-and-white wingtip. “I came to this country to pursue my education,” the caption read. “Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg,” he said, “carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience.” “I mean, Pierre would have been a model citizen,” Jack said now, driving Renee and his mom toward another part of the route that he needed to see. “He had so much going for him. I think there’s more to the story than they’re saying.” He said he knew there was more because of how the state troopers had described what happened in their preliminary report. It said that Pierre had “walked” into traffic, whereas Jack had told them that “he ran at me like a damn football player.” He kept replaying the moment. “I didn’t see him until the last minute—when I got up to him, it was just timed perfectly,” he said. “That’s what I’m saying. That’s what don’t make any sense.” “It was a coincidence,” Renee said. “Maybe it was, but it was just all timed too perfectly,” Jack continued. “You’d have to be in my shoes to see that. But I keep on thinking about it.” Renee kept telling him that he was rationalizing. That he was traumatized. But in the days after Pierre’s death, Jack had kept going. He reviewed what he knew about Haiti, which was gangs, killings, and corruption. The only Haitian Jack knew was a girl Renee’s aunt and uncle had adopted as a baby when they were missionaries over there. They had told him what it was like. He reviewed what he knew about the Haitians in Springfield, which had mostly come from his mother, via a friend of hers who lived there, and had little good to say; Jack had seen a video she’d circulated purporting to show Haitians eating cats and dogs. Diana had called her up after everything happened, and her friend had sworn that Pierre had waited on her at Texas Roadhouse the weekend before. The friend said she recognized him from the photos. She told Diana that she and her husband had ordered two salads, and when the waiter she assumed was Pierre brought only one salad, she told him that they’d ordered two; she said that he had smiled and said something in a language she did not understand. Diana still wondered about what he’d said. She told Jack that she was worried about him, that Haitians in Springfield were angry. That everybody in the country seemed to be angry, including her. “My son could have died,” she said now. “A whole bunch of lives could have been taken. And that’s another thing—” “No,” Renee said, attempting to preempt what she knew was coming. “That’s why I think this is a statement—some kind of statement,” Diana continued. “It’s not a statement,” Renee said. “It is. Look how it’s blowing out,” Diana said, referring to all the news and the vitriol toward the Trump administration. “No,” Renee said. But Diana, who had spent years working as a nurse in Ohio prisons, continued. She said her experience had taught her to think “outside the box,” and she offered a theory that none of the investigating authorities had suggested. She believed that what happened could have been more than a suicide, that Pierre could have been “almost like a suicide bomber,” attempting to send a political message. She said she believed that this could start happening more often. “I’ve seen stuff on the internet too—like, someone said, ‘You should be thinking of the truck driver too,’ and someone commented, ‘Oh, fuck that truck driver,’” Diana said. Carol Guzy for The Atlantic Bel had recently graduated from high school, where he’d been a soccer player and member of Junior ROTC. She had been worried enough to contact Carl Ruby, the pastor in Springfield, to hear more about the situation there. He had told her that Haitians had been losing their jobs since Trump revoked their legal status, and were terrified of being sent back to Haiti, where deportees were being targeted because gangs assumed they had money. He told her they found the ankle monitors humiliating. He also told her that he had been with Pierre’s father the night his son died and had gone with him to view his son’s body. He said that the family had no animosity toward her or Jack, and that they understood he had done everything in his power to avoid the collision. Ruby, who told me that it was a “really good talk,” told Diana that he was sorry for what her son had been through, and invited them both to come to one of the vigils that had been happening almost every night since Pierre’s death. Diana had asked Ruby to pass on their condolences to the family, but she did not think it was a good idea to show up. Jack had thought about going; some part of him wanted to go. “I feel really bad for the family,” he said now, getting closer to the stop on his route that he wanted to see. “I just don’t want to take the chance for the safety of my family. I mean, he jumped out in front of me. But I still killed their son.” “You feel guilty about it,” Renee said. “I feel guilty,” Jack said. “I hate to say it, but there’s a lot of animosity against, just, white people,” Diana said. “I’m sorry.” “That’s not our belief, Diana,” Renee said. “I put my pistol out, just in case—you never know,” Jack said. He exited the highway in Westerville, the stop on the route where he delivers concrete powder twice a day, and drove over to a complex of metal chutes and silos. Right after everything happened, he had been talking with a friend who found out that Westerville had an ICE field office that Pierre had visited, and now Jack put the address into Google Maps and navigated over to a brick building 1.7 miles away. He tried to imagine Pierre getting fitted with the ankle monitor and, in the weeks before his death, showing up at the field office and pleading to get it taken off. Jack imagined this happening right down the street from where he was going about his job. “It was so close,” he said, looking at the building. “It don’t make sense in my mind. I’m trying to come up with a reason.” Renee told him it was just a coincidence. “It could be a coincidence, it could,” he said. “Maybe my intuition is telling me something.” He wondered whether Pierre might have noticed his truck as he drove through Westerville. “My truck is 23 years old—it’s not something you see on the road every day. I think, at some point, we’d get off at the same exit and get on at the same exit,” he said, turning back onto the highway. He started replaying everything that had happened. Seeing the car, seeing Pierre get out, seeing Pierre run toward his truck. And then he recalled another detail about that moment. “He made eye contact,” Jack said now. “He was looking at your truck, not you ,” Renee said. “Renee, he made eye contact,” Jack said. “He looked me dead in the eyes.” T hey headed toward home. Chillicothe was an hour from Springfield, but to Jack what was happening there felt closer now. Since ICE operations began in early August, locals have witnessed agents in unmarked SUVs with dark windows detain people at apartment complexes, strip-mall parking lots, gas stations, a car wash, and frequently during traffic stops. At least 74 people, nearly all Haitians, almost none with criminal convictions, have been detained so far, according to lawyers and local activists. Dozens more, they said, have been fitted with ankle monitors, including pregnant women and elderly people. Carol Guzy Monsanto Maler, who came to the U.S. from Haiti in 2023, became emotional and fell to the ground after receiving an ankle monitor at an ICE check-in in Blue Ash, Ohio, in August. When I visited in early September, much of the Haitian community was in hiding. Families were getting food delivered to their homes, attending church services online. Haitian activists told me that some people had spoken of suicide as an alternative to deportation. At the vigils for Pierre, the people who showed up included his high-school teachers, his soccer coaches and teammates, waiters from Texas Roadhouse, and others who described themselves as neighbors, including a man who told a crowd one night that Pierre’s death was “a failing of broader policy, but I will always bear the guilt that there is more that I could have done and we could have done.” What is happening has been transformative for some people, including Carl Ruby. His congregation, Central Christian Church, has been actively supporting the Haitian community since 2024, when Vice President Vance and others started spreading the false stories about Haitians eating cats and dogs. On the Monday night after Pierre’s death, Ruby told me, he’d sat with Ronal Bel as he talked to reporters with a stoicism that Ruby could not fathom, then followed him into a closet, where Ronal broke down. A few days later, when Ruby accompanied him to a local funeral home, he watched as Ronal walked circles around the table where his son’s body lay and repeated, “You have been a good son.” At one point, Ronal took off his shirt and waved it over his son’s body, which Ruby understood as a ritual that meant “I want my spirit to go with you. I’m not abandoning you.” Viles Dorsainvil, the executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, who has been spending time with Ronal, told me, “He’s still having questions, and it’s hard for him to accept if he’s living in this reality.” Yesterday, Ronal Bel sat in the front row at St. John Missionary Baptist Church for his son’s funeral. He asked a family friend to read his recollections of his first-born son, who had grown up in the port city of Aux Cayes, along the southern coast of Haiti. “I feel like I have lost everything,” the friend read. “I just cannot sleep” and “When someone opens the front door, I have the sense that it is him, coming home.” Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican, who has taken multiple humanitarian trips to Haiti and has criticized Trump’s effort to deport Haitians as “a mistake,” was among those in the pews, sitting alongside Haitians and other people from Springfield and beyond. Addressing the crowd, Dorsainvil said that Ronal Bel had come to the U.S. after surviving a massacre in Haiti, and that his son’s life is “part of a larger human story. ” He said that the mourning “extends beyond one family.” Ruby spoke of the different circles of people affected by Pierre’s death—those closest to him, neighbors in Springfield who want Haitian families to know that “you are a blessing and not a burden to this community,” and another group, those who are “curious and just want to reach a better understanding of what happened to Damas. Some, even though they don’t know your family and are not part of this community, want you to know that they share your grief.” Carol Guzy for The Atlantic Students and staff honor Bel at Wright State University, where he had just started college, on September 8. In the two weeks before the funeral, Jack had gone back to work. He returned to his regular route, avoiding the right lane as he passed through the stretch of cornfields and wildflowers. One Saturday morning, he and Renee were at his mother’s house in Chillicothe, still trying to piece things together. “Maybe you just felt like he made eye contact,” Renee was saying to him. “I know he did. I don’t know why,” Jack said. “I think you were affected by this more than you want to admit,” Renee said, and then Jack mentioned that the other truck driver, the one who had pried him from his cab, had called him. He and the man, John Hallings, had exchanged phone numbers at the scene that day and had been talking off and on since then, Hallings told me. He was a trained emergency responder and had a medical kit in his truck. He had gotten out of his cab with gloves on, kneeled in front of Jack’s truck, and checked for Pierre’s pulse, which was gone. “He went straight to that boy,” Jack said. “He said it kind of messed him up. He’s not doing so hot.” Hallings had told Jack that he’d gotten extremely depressed thinking about Pierre, and then extremely angry thinking that he could have killed more people than just himself, and thinking about immigrants taking jobs in the trucking industry, bringing down wages. Then, a few days after that, he had broken down crying. “He said he was kind of worried about me,” Jack said, checking his phone for any more details about Pierre. “You shouldn’t look so much,” Renee said. “But, Renee, I care ,” Jack said. He said that the more he learned about Pierre, the more he was beginning to understand. He’d recently found out, for instance, that Pierre had been a kind of leader in his family. Besides bringing in money, those who knew him had talked about how he was the one in his family who spoke the best English, who could fill out forms, make phone calls, and otherwise help his family manage their lives in Springfield. “I think he just had a lot piled on his shoulders,” Jack said. He himself had been caring for an ailing father for the past 15 years, bathing him, helping him recover after two strokes. “I’d say the boy was stressed. I’d say he’d probably had enough.” “I wish I would have known him, because I would have taken him in,” Diana said at one point. “I got a spare room.” “I think a lot of people would have helped him,” Jack said. He had kept thinking about the ankle monitor, to the point that he went online one night to find out more about the devices. “His was a dinosaur—it was big ,” Jack said. “My sister’s ex had one,” Renee said. “Pierre’s was ginormous,” Jack said, calling up a photo of one on his phone. [ Read: A reverse Ellis Island ] He had tried to imagine how Pierre had felt walking around with it on, attempting to play soccer, and he had learned something else about the ICE monitor that really bothered him, which was that Pierre had to keep it charged himself. “And if he let it go dead, he gets in trouble. I mean, it’s a joke,” Jack said. “I mean, come on, you got a decorated kid, a full-time student, playing soccer, and they’re going to do that shit to him? I think he just probably felt defeated. He put all that effort in, and he wasn’t getting anywhere. And being from a Third World country too? We don’t know what those people walk in day-to-day.” “I’m not trying to sound mean or anything, but we can’t take care of everybody,” Diana said. “Well, we wouldn’t have had to take care of Pierre. Pierre was doing what he was supposed to do,” Jack said. “We did not do right by him.” He was beginning to believe that the Trump administration was “a joke,” and that the Democrats were no better. “Everything is broken,” Jack said. He started going over it all again. The morning that began so normally. The cornfields and wildflowers. A young Haitian man named Pierre Damas Bel whose troubles had become his own. He kept imagining Pierre looking him dead in the eyes. “He was hurting,” Jack said. He recalled the moment right after that. “If I had just swerved a little sooner,” he said. “I wish I could’ve done more to keep that truck off him.” And the moment right after that. “I felt a big thump, and I knew it was him,” he said. “I could feel it all.” Renee reached for his hand, knowing that he was feeling it still. “I’m good, I’m good,” the truck driver said. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, you can call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org for more resources.

Como ya advertía la Aemet, la previsión está sujeta a mucha incertidumbre y en cualquier momento pueden producirse lluvias de mayor intensidad de la prevista en puntos donde no se esperaba, como ocurrió el sábado en Madrigueras (Albacete) . items.title: Algérie : Abdelmadjid Tebboune exprime l’ambition d’atteindre un PIB de 400 milliards de dollars fin 2026 ou début 2027
items.description: Dans un entretien avec les representants de la presse algerienne, diffuse sur la chaîne nationale le 3 octobre, le president Abdelmadjid Tebboune a declare qu'il est « envisageable » pour l'Algerie d'atteindre un produit interieur brut (PIB) de 400 milliards de dollars « a la fin de 2026 ou au cours du premier trimestre de 2027 ». « Il est meme possible de depasser ce chiffre, comme le confirme le Fonds monetaire international (FMI) », a-t-il ajoute, justifiant cette perspective par « la dynamique de l'investissement, qui se concretise a travers des milliers de projets a l'echelle nationale ainsi que par la valorisation du potentiel de plusieurs secteurs ». Dynamique de redefinition des structures economiques algeriennes L'ambition du president algerien emanerait d'une dynamique agressive d'investissement, de relance des projets miniers et de renforcement des industries dans le cadre d'une politique economique visant a s'affranchir progressivement de la rente petroliere. L'investissement productif est place au centre de la strategie du gouvernement pour creer de la valeur via ses entreprises, son industrie et ses infrastructures avec plus de 20 000 projets d'investissement, recenses par l'Agence algerienne de promotion de l'investissement (AAPI), qui representent une valeur globale declaree superieure a 9 000 milliards de dinars (plus de 67,5 milliards de dollars), qui devrait generer plus de 525 000 emplois directs. Les variables macroeconomiques qui pourraient depasser les previsions du FMI Apres avoir estime la croissance algerienne a 3,9 % en 2025, le FMI a revu ce chiffre legerement a la baisse, a 3,8 % en 2026. Le president algerien a cependant estime que cette prevision ne tenait pas compte de la rapidite d'execution des nouvelles usines, du raccordement strategique des sites miniers aux reseaux de transport et de la disponibilite croissante d'intrants industriels locaux, autant de facteurs qui ne sont pas inclus dans les methodes de calcul internationales mais qui pourraient impacter significativement les chiffres de la croissance. Abdelmadjid Tebboune a, par ailleurs, souligne que le taux de croissance realise par l'economie algerienne depassait celui enregistre par certains pays en Europe et autour de la Mediterranee.

items.title: Ashaiman Assembly deploys monitoring system to curb dumping in storm drain
items.description: The Ashaiman Municipal Assembly (ASHMA) has marked World Cleanup Day with an intensive three-in-one sanitation and dredging exercise targeting chronic environmental challenges along the major Gbeblemɛ storm drain at the New Town Bridge. Leading the exercise, the Ashaiman Municipal Chief Executive (MCE), Mr Freeman Tsekpo, expressed deep concern over the misuse of municipal water channels by residents who had turned sections of the storm drain into unauthorised refuse dumps. Addressing assembly staff, machine operators and community members, he outlined a two-pronged strategy to permanently address the sanitation challenge. “We are using extra hands and heavy machinery to make sure that we remove all the refuse dumped at the site; secondly, we are setting up a satellite monitoring system here so that after this exercise, we will not see this kind of abuse again,” he said. As part of community policing initiatives, the MCE announced that local pig farmers operating near the area had been engaged to act as environmental wardens to deter illegal dumping. Speaking on the structural status of the critical waterway, he noted that the Gbeblemɛ channel serves as the primary storm drain for Ashaiman and falls under the jurisdiction of the Hydrological Services Department of the Ministry of Works and Housing. The MCE reiterated the Assembly’s continuous lobbying efforts to upgrade the ageing earth drain into a modern, fully constructed concrete storm drain. He noted that previous overflows, which caused major floods in 2010 and 2018, as well as minor incidents up to 2024, had severely threatened residents. He, however, highlighted that massive dredging and desilting works undertaken at the Adjei-Kojo exit point had successfully prevented severe flooding during recent seasonal rains. Mr Tsekpo acknowledged that pressure on local sanitation infrastructure remains exceptionally high, with Ashaiman’s population exceeding 300,000 alongside intense commercial activity. To address the challenge, he said the Assembly was aggressively promoting waste segregation by separating plastic and organic waste, supported by municipal partnerships with smart plastic recycling networks and firms such as Safisana, which converts organic waste and faecal matter into electricity. He commended assembly members, unit committee members and residents for supporting concurrent clean-up exercises across various electoral areas to safeguard public health and promote sustainable municipal development.

items.title: John Boadu must rebuild, unite NPP for 2028 – Edward Boateng
items.description: Former Ghanaian Ambassador to China, Edward Boateng, has tasked the newly elected National Chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), John Boadu, with rebuilding and uniting the party ahead of the 2028 general elections. Mr Boateng said Mr Boadu’s election comes with a significant responsibility to strengthen the NPP’s organisational structures, restore discipline and rebuild public confidence in the party. “The task ahead goes beyond administering the Party. As Chairman, he must lead the rebuilding of a strong, disciplined and effective political organisation, from the polling station to the national level,” he said. “Chairman John Boadu has served the Party at virtually every level and understands its strengths, weaknesses and grassroots structures. The task now is to build a united and formidable Party capable of supporting our Flagbearer, winning back the confidence of Ghanaians and returning the NPP to government in 2029,” he added. According to him, the party must learn from its defeat in the 2024 general elections and undertake a deliberate effort to reconnect with its grassroots and the Ghanaian electorate. Mr Boateng also called for reconciliation among the various traditions and tendencies within the NPP, saying members who supported different candidates during the national elections must be brought together to contribute to the party’s rebuilding. He said the task ahead requires unity, humility, hard work, fresh thinking and a compelling message capable of reconnecting the NPP with Ghanaians. Mr Boateng highlighted Mr Boadu’s experience at various levels of the party, including his service as National Organiser and Acting General Secretary between 2014 and 2016. He said Mr Boadu’s experience in the party’s grassroots structures would be critical to the rebuilding process. John Boadu was elected National Chairman at the NPP’s National Delegates Conference at the Baba Yara Sports Stadium in Kumasi on Saturday, October 3. He secured 2,888 votes to defeat Boakye Kyerematen Agyarko, who polled 2,408 votes. Former National Chairman Paul Afoko received 790 votes, while Sammy Crabbe obtained 41 votes. Mr Boateng said the new leadership must now work collectively to build a united and formidable party capable of supporting the NPP’s Flagbearer, Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, ahead of the 2028 elections.

items.title: Cheikh Hamidou Kane s’en est allé, démontrant encore une fois, l’ambiguïté de notre aventure
items.description: Avec la disparition de Cheikh Hamidou Kane, le Sénégal perd l’une de ses grandes figures intellectuelles. Écrivain, philosophe et haut fonctionnaire, son œuvre aura perpétuellement nourri la lancinante question, entre l’influence de la tradition africaine d’un côté et la modernité occidentale de l’autre. Cheikh Hamidou Kane a connu une trajectoire littéraire non prolifique mais fabuleuse, dont L’Aventure ambiguë, publiée en 1961, restera l’expression littéraire la plus éclatante. Cheikh Hamidou Kane est né le 2 avril 1928 à Matam. Il est d’abord encadré en l’enseignement coranique avant de rejoindre l’école française. Après le baccalauréat obtenu au lycée Van Vollenhoven de Dakar, il poursuit ses études à l’Institut des Hautes Études de Dakar, avant de rejoindre Paris. Au lycée Louis-le-Grand puis à la Sorbonne, il étudie le droit et la philosophie et obtient deux licences. Il complète cette formation par l’École nationale de la France d’Outre-Mer, dont il sort breveté en 1959. De retour au Sénégal, il occupera plusieurs fonctions administratives. Gouverneur de la région de Thiès, Haut-Commissaire général au Plan, il poursuit ensuite une importante carrière internationale, notamment à l’UNICEF, où il devient directeur régional pour l’Afrique subsaharienne. Il exercera également des responsabilités au Centre de recherches pour le développement international, avant de devenir ministre du Développement industriel et de l’Artisanat, puis ministre du Plan et de la Coopération. «L’Aventure ambiguë» est publié en 1961. Cheikh Hamidou Kane reconnaîtra lui-même que l’itinéraire de Samba Diallo, principal personnage du roman est étroitement lié à sa propre expérience. À travers cette œuvre, Cheikh Hamidou Kane pose une question qui demeure encore l’une des grandes interrogations intellectuelles de l’Afrique. Comment accéder au savoir et à la modernité sans perdre son identité ? Le roman met ainsi en scène la confrontation entre tradition et modernité, mais également celle entre deux systèmes éducatifs. L’enseignement coranique de Thierno vise la formation spirituelle de l’homme. L’école occidentale apporte les sciences et les instruments de compréhension du monde moderne. Un seul livre pendant plus de trente ans La particularité de Cheikh Hamidou Kane tient aussi à son rapport à l’écriture. Il n’a jamais été un auteur fécond. Pendant plus de trois décennies, « L’Aventure ambiguë » restera pratiquement son seul roman. Publié en 1961, il lui assure rapidement une renommée internationale et reçoit le Grand Prix littéraire d’Afrique noire en 1962. Cette rareté se justifie peut être. Cheikh Hamidou Kane avait également choisi de consacrer une grande partie de son existence à l’action publique, au développement et aux responsabilités internationales. Son silence littéraire n’était donc pas nécessairement une fuite. Il pouvait aussi être une forme de choix et de fidélité à un questionnement solidement implanté. Il faudra attendre 1995, soit trente-quatre ans après « L’Aventure ambiguë », pour voir paraître « Les Gardiens du Temple », son deuxième et dernier roman. Deux romans en plus de trois décennies, une bibliographie courte, mais une empreinte considérable. « L’Aventure ambiguë » apparaît comme bien plus qu’un roman. C’est l’œuvre d’une éternité, entrer à jamais dans l’histoire, son auteur avec. O.BA

items.title: Executive intimidation of opposition undermines separation of powers – Prof Oquaye
items.description: Former Speaker of Parliament, Prof. Aaron Mike Oquaye, has cautioned that the principle of separation of powers is undermined when the Executive uses state institutions to intimidate or silence members of the opposition. According to him, parliamentary privilege and constitutional protections must be respected regardless of the political party involved. Prof. Oquaye stressed that protecting parliamentary privilege is essential to maintaining the constitutional balance between the arms of government. “You cannot have separation of powers in the Constitution if the Executive takes steps to shut up the opposition, and that harassment is not good,” he said. Prof. Oquaye made the remarks while explaining his handling of a case involving former MP for Bawku Central, Mahama Ayariga, who was wanted by the Office of the Special Prosecutor during his tenure as Speaker. He said his intervention was based on the need to protect Mr Ayariga’s constitutional rights, rather than partisan considerations. “Honourable Ayariga was wanted by the previous Special Prosecutor during my tenure. I was very, very, very active in stopping the attempts because, you see, it is not a matter of NPP or NDC,” he said. Prof. Oquaye said he invited the then Special Prosecutor to an open meeting to ensure that the matter was handled in accordance with the Constitution. “I was very, very, very much insistent on protecting his rights. So much so that I invited the Special Prosecutor for an open meeting, so that we all follow the tenets of the Constitution. “I supported it with a letter for the records. It’s there. And Ayariga would not be abused. His rights would not be abused,” Prof. Oquaye said. He added, “If you read my ruling, as journalists go investigate. I traced the history of parliamentary privilege, including the infractions that took place even in England, and how it came to be strengthened, and the purpose behind it.”

items.title: 10 footballers who served in military before football fame
items.description: Football has produced some of the world’s biggest sporting stars, but several prominent footballers also have military backgrounds. From mandatory national service to active military duty, these footballers served in the armed forces before or during their professional careers. Here are 10 notable footballers who were former military personnel. 1. Son Heung-min South Korea captain Son Heung-min completed his mandatory military service with the Republic of Korea Marine Corps in 2020. His service was shortened to about three weeks after he helped South Korea win the gold medal at the 2018 Asian Games, which earned the squad an exemption from the country’s standard lengthy military service requirement. 2. Eric Cantona Former Manchester United and France forward Eric Cantona completed two years of compulsory military service in the French Army. Cantona later established himself as one of the most influential players in Manchester United’s history. 3. Sir Bobby Charlton England and Manchester United legend Sir Bobby Charlton served in the Royal Army Ordnance Corps during his national service. He also represented the British Army football team before going on to win the 1966 World Cup with England. 4. Duncan Edwards Manchester United great Duncan Edwards also served in the Royal Army Ordnance Corps. The midfielder completed his military service while beginning his professional football career and went on to become one of the most highly regarded players of his generation. 5. Paolo Maldini Italy and AC Milan legend Paolo Maldini completed compulsory military service in the Italian Army. Maldini subsequently enjoyed a career spanning more than two decades with AC Milan and the Italy national team. 6. Fabio Cannavaro Former Italy captain Fabio Cannavaro served in the Italian military between 1995 and 1996. The defender later captained Italy to victory at the 2006 FIFA World Cup and won the Ballon d’Or that same year. 7. Gary Holt Former Scotland international Gary Holt served in the Army Catering Corps and played for the British Army football team. He later built a professional career that included spells with Norwich City and Kilmarnock. 8. Teemu Tainio Former Tottenham Hotspur midfielder Teemu Tainio completed military service in the Finnish Defence Forces. The Finland international later played in France and England, including for Tottenham and Sunderland. 9. Bruce Grobbelaar Former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar was conscripted into the Rhodesian Army in 1975. He served during the Rhodesian Bush War before establishing himself as Liverpool’s first-choice goalkeeper and helping the club win several major trophies. 10. Gordon Astall Former England international Gordon Astall served in the Royal Marines during World War II. After his military service, he continued his football career and represented England at international level. The post 10 footballers who served in military before football fame appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: France : un adolescent de 15 ans déféré après l’agression d’une passante en marge des manifestations lycéennes
items.description: Un adolescent de quinze ans et demi soupçonné d'avoir actionné un spray enflammé sur le visage d'une passante à Marseille en marge des manifestations lycéennes a été déféré dimanche en vue de sa mise en examen pour « acte de barbarie », a annoncé le parquet. Une vidéo de l'agression, qui s'est déroulée jeudi matin sur une place de Marseille, a circulé sur les réseaux sociaux. Elle montre la femme de 40 ans, auxiliaire de vie, s'interposer au moment où un groupe tente de fracasser un abribus « dans un contexte de manifestations lycéennes aux abords du lycée Colbert », indique le parquet. Visage masqué, le mineur s'avance alors vers la femme et projette « en direction de son visage un spray qu'il enflammait à l'aide d'un briquet », selon la source. Le communiqué précise que l'adolescent est élève au lycée Colbert, « en seconde service d'aide à la personne », et rappelle qu'il était inconnu des services de police et de justice. Interpellé vendredi soir et placé en garde à vue, il « reconnaissait immédiatement les faits et, en saisissant la portée, exprimait de profonds regrets », précise encore le parquet. Dimanche, il a été « déféré en vue de sa mise en examen par un juge d'instruction du chef d'acte de barbarie », ajoute le parquet, qui a demandé son placement en détention provisoire. Interrogée par BFMTV, la victime, soignée pour des brûlures au visage, a raconté avoir tenté de dissuader un groupe de jeunes filles qui voulait fracasser l'abribus. « Je leur ai dit : +Mais qu'est-ce que vous faites, vous n'allez rien casser du tout, allez manifester+ », a-t-elle dit dans un entretien diffusé samedi soir. « Je ne m'attendais pas à une telle violence », a-t-elle témoigné. « Voir un gamin qu'on ne connaît pas, avec qui on parlait normalement, qui vous vise délibérément au visage… Il n'a pas visé les habits, il n'a pas visé les jambes. Il m'a visé au visage. Pourquoi ? ». items.title: Agoè-Nyivé/Togo Propre : Une mobilisation citoyenne dans la commune Agoè-Nyivé 2
items.description: Agoè-Nyivé, 4 oct. (ATOP) – La population de la commune Agoè-Nyivé 2 s’est mobilisée, le samedi 3 octobre, dans le cadre de l’opération nationale « Togo Propre ». Munis de balais, houes, coupe-coupe, paniers, pelles et râteaux, les habitants, les agents de la mairie, les responsables, des CVD ont investi plusieurs espaces, notamment les abords du marché de Légbassito, pour participer à l’assainissement de leur cadre de vie. La population L’opération, organisée dans les différentes communes du pays, vise à renforcer la salubrité publique et à promouvoir la participation citoyenne à la protection de l’environnement. À Agoè-Nyivé 2, l’activité a connu la participation du préfet d’Agoè-Nyivé, Dr Tinaka Wédiabalo Kossi, venu aux côtés des populations pour prendre part aux travaux de salubrité. Les participants se sont attelés au balayage, au désherbage, au ramassage des déchets et au nettoyage des espaces publics. Le préfet a salué la mobilisation et l’engagement de la population. Il a encouragé les habitants à maintenir cet élan au-delà de la journée de Togo Propre, en adoptant des comportements responsables et en veillant quotidiennement à la propreté de leur environnement. Cette opération a également été l’occasion de rappeler que la préservation de la salubrité publique constitue une responsabilité partagée entre les autorités locales et les citoyens. La participation active des populations contribue ainsi à rendre les quartiers, marchés et espaces publics plus propres et plus agréables. L’opération « Togo Propre » s’est déroulée simultanément dans les différentes communes de la préfecture, avec la mobilisation des autorités, des collectivités territoriales et des populations. items.title: Reproduction et embouche ovine: Le Fonstab injecte plus de 500 millions de FCFA à Kaolack
items.description: Le ministre chargé de l’Élevage, Ousmane Diagne, a présidé, samedi 03 octobre 2026 à Kaolack, une cérémonie de remise de chèques de financement et d’attestations de formation aux bénéficiaires du programme de reproduction et d’embouche ovine. Plus de 500 millions de francs CFA ont été mobilisés au profit de coopératives et de groupements d’intérêt économique (GIE). Portée par le Fonds d’appui à la stabulation (Fonstab), en partenariat avec l’Office national de formation professionnelle (ONFP) et Heifer International, l’initiative vise à renforcer la production ovine et les capacités des acteurs. Les financements sont destinés à soutenir le développement des activités des bénéficiaires. « Derrière ces attestations et ces financements, il y a des hommes et des femmes aptes à se prendre en charge. Cette démarche s’inscrit dans la dynamique de renforcer la production nationale et d’intensifier la modernisation de l’élevage », a déclaré l’administratrice générale du Fonstab, Mme Diouf, née Fatou Diop Bakhoum. Selon elle, le Fonstab compte à ce jour 5 549 projets financés, pour un montant global de 21,4 milliards de francs CFA. Le programme a également permis de renforcer les capacités de 750 bénéficiaires. Les formations ont notamment porté sur la reproduction et l’embouche ovine, la gestion des exploitations et l’alimentation animale. Le dispositif repose sur trois leviers, à savoir la formation, le financement et le suivi. Il met également l’accent sur les cultures fourragères, la santé animale et la commercialisation. Le ministre chargé de l’Élevage a salué cette initiative, estimant qu’elle permettra d’accroître la production nationale, d’améliorer les revenus des éleveurs et de mieux valoriser les ressources. Ousmane Diagne a invité les bénéficiaires à respecter leurs engagements, notamment en matière de remboursement. « Chaque projet réussi, chaque financement remboursé permettra à d’autres jeunes, d’autres femmes et d’autres coopératives d’accéder, à leur tour, à ce dispositif », a-t-il souligné. Mamadou THIAM (Correspondant)

items.title: Haho/Sécurité routière : Les populations et organisations des syndicats des conducteurs routiers sensibilisées
items.description: Notsè, 4 oct. (ATOP) – Les responsables et organisations des syndicats des conducteurs routiers de la commune Haho1 ont été sensibilisés, le vendredi 2 octobre à Notsè sur la sécurité routière et les stationnements anarchiques. A l’actif de la commune Haho 1, cette rencontre vise à attirer l’attention des usagers de la route et de la population sur les risques liés aux non-respects du code de la route, le surcharge des véhicules, les transports mixtes, le stationnement anarchique dans la commune et les traversées maladroites des voies par les piétons. Les participants ont suivi des présentations sur les faits atroces et des cas d’accidents dus à l’inattention des chauffeurs, le non-respect des règles élémentaires du code de la route, des stationnements non contrôlés et des traversées anarchiques des personnes. Le tableau sombre des accidents de la circulation privant ainsi la vie à des milliers de personnes a été également présentée. Selon le chef de la Division sécurité routière (DSR- Notsè), Alayi Caladom, les drames sont souvent causés par des excès des vitesses, des défauts de maîtrise de l’engin, des dépassement défectueux, le non-respect des feux tricolores et le refus des priorités. Il a convié la population à la vigilance et la mise en pratique des règles élémentaires de la route. Le maire de la commune Haho 1, Koffi Assila a déclaré que la mairie Haho 1 entend poursuivre la sensibilisation avec les responsables et organisations des syndicats des conducteurs routiers et la population afin de réduire les stationnements anarchiques qui sont aussi cause d’insécurité routière. ATOP/YM/SED/KYA

items.title: A TV Show Where Teens Actually Act Like Teens
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Marie-Rose Sheinerman, an assistant editor who has written about President Trump’s spree to put his face on everything , the administration’s boat-strike campaign , and ICE showing up at family court . Marie-Rose is adamant about recommending The Sopranos to her friends. She also enjoys listening to Natalia Lafourcade’s Tiny Desk concert, visiting the 2,000-year-old crocodile statue at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and rewatching Moonstruck . — Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor The television show I’m most enjoying right now: I first watched The Sopranos during the height of the coronavirus pandemic and have been on a continuous loop of rewatches more or less since. To the people in my life who somehow have yet to experience it, despite my persistent recommendations: “ One thing you can never say: that you haven’t been told .” The show has it all—the banality of evil, the corrosive cruelty of a certain vision of masculinity, the crushing weight of American decline. It also has pounds of gabagool, Paulie Walnuts’s chuckle, an intervention led by “the guy who broke into Stew Leonard’s that time,” and some of the funniest lines ever aired on television. The last thing that made me laugh: Olivia Wilde’s The Invite —a dramedy about an ill-fated foursome, set almost entirely in the confines of one apartment—marked the last time I snorted from laughter in a theater . The last time I snorted from laughter, in general, would be about 90 minutes prior to writing this, when I was rewatching an episode from the first season of Derry Girls . Lisa McGee’s Netflix show is about a group of teenage friends in Northern Ireland, set against the backdrop of the Troubles. What’s special about the series is that it has the rare quality of immersing its viewers in the unvarnished perspectives of kids who talk and act like real kids, without becoming a show for kids. The last thing that made me cry: I saw Death of a Salesman starring Nathan Lane on Broadway in May, and it’s hard to imagine that another theater experience this year will surpass its emotional impact. Laurie Metcalf’s performance as Linda Loman, in particular, left me deeply moved. An author I will read anything by: When it’s publication day for Rachel Aviv at The New Yorker , not much else is getting done until I’m through with reading her latest. A quiet song that I love, and a loud song that I love: I apologize for bending the rules by offering several quiet songs by way of Natalia Lafourcade’s Tiny Desk concert . To evoke whatever the opposite of Lafourcadian quiet is, try “Somebody to Love,” by Jefferson Airplane. Part of my love for the song comes from its use in Joel and Ethan Coen’s A Serious Man —my personal pick for a single piece of American Jewish art to take with me to a deserted island. A work of art that I cherish: I have loved this 2,000-year-old crocodile since my grandmother started taking me to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, specifically its Egyptian Art wing, as one of our primary afternoon activities when I was a kid. It’s hard to say what is so special about it, but when I think about the countless hours I spent with her in those halls, first in a stroller and later walking next to her, I think of that crocodile statue. Something I recently revisited: I think my happiest two hours of the past two weeks were the ones spent rewatching Cher and Nicolas Cage’s Moonstruck . And if you still haven’t?! Snap out of it! A piece of journalism that recently changed my perspective on a topic: David Armstrong’s “ The Price of Remission ,” published by ProPublica, has come to mind on many occasions, in many contexts, since I first read it last year. The story follows Armstrong’s journey, after receiving a cancer diagnosis, to understand why a single capsule of his daily medication costs 25 cents to make yet is priced at nearly $1,000. It’s a tremendous feat of personal writing and investigative journalism, and it pried open my understanding of the individuals and systems that keep health-care costs astronomically high in the United States. It also offers a window into the cycles of hope and heartbreak that govern breakthroughs in cancer research; for more of that, I highly recommend Siddhartha Mukherjee’s The Emperor of All Maladies: A Biography of Cancer . A favorite story I’ve read in The Atlantic : Limiting myself to one is an extremely tall order, but I might choose Stephanie McCrummen’s story in the August issue: “ The Demon Next Door .” It’s a master class in unearthing startling facts and in constructing startling sentences. My favorite way of wasting time on my phone: There are two rabbit holes I have, unfortunately, tumbled down—one human, the other not, but both topsy-turvy in ways that Lewis Carroll could not have foreseen. For more than a year now, when I’ve wanted to dial my brain down, the Queen of RichTok’s Instagram has proved a reliable resource. Videos by Becca Bloom, as Rebecca Ma is known online, are hard to look away from—she occupies an uncanny world where she wears custom Van Cleef & Arpels while feeding a breakfast bowl of caviar, edible flowers, and salmon sashimi to her cat. The cat’s name is Oscar, and I’m as familiar with his diet as I am with that of my roommate. The other rabbit hole deposits me in the mysterious world of love and betrayal among AI-generated fruit. To borrow a turn of phrase that Riverdale applied to high-school football , you’ve either experienced the epic highs and lows of Bananito and Strawberrina’s whirlwind affairs, or you haven’t—and I’ll leave it at that. A good recommendation I recently received: Virginia Evans’s debut novel, The Correspondent , was recommended to me by not one but two colleagues, and it did not disappoint. A poem, or line of poetry, that I return to: There’s a strong argument to be made that childhood begins to end the moment you realize that your parents are—and, even more remarkably, always were—people with anxieties and obligations and dreams of their own, much like the person you are becoming now. “The Raincoat,” by Ada Limón , is a poem I first encountered the summer after graduating high school; each time I have read it since, I’ve been struck by it all over again. Limón’s narrator, while driving home from a medical appointment, reflects on how her mother took her to scores of such appointments as a kid, during which she never asked her mother “what she gave up to drive me, / or how her day was before this chore.” Then, she spots a mother taking off her own rain jacket to shield her daughter from a storm: My god, I thought, my whole life I’ve been under her raincoat thinking it was somehow a marvel that I never got wet. Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic : Why Americans stopped throwing dinner parties The great data-center rebellion The babies left behind in America The Week Ahead Other Mommy , a horror film about a mother and the sinister entity that begins impersonating her (in theaters Friday) Small Prophets , a comedy series about a man who turns to alchemy to solve the mystery of his girlfriend’s disappearance (streaming Wednesday on Apple TV) Partita , a novel by Barbara Kingsolver about a rural woman and the classical-music career she left behind (out Tuesday) Essay Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic. Sources: Courtesy of TIFF The 14 Movies to Look Out for This Fall By Shirley Li The Princess Bride . The Shawshank Redemption . Almost Famous . Over the course of its 51-year history, the Toronto International Film Festival has hosted notable films of all genres and styles. The 2026 edition, which concluded in mid-September, curated movies from rising talent and established filmmakers alike, including a modern-day Nigerian-set remake of Mrs. Dalloway , a gorgeous coming-of-age drama about a school trip to Pompeii, and a rollicking comedy about a community-theater troupe attempting to stage a musical. Below are 14 of my favorite films from the ones I caught, most of which will arrive in theaters in the coming months. Read the full article.
