items.title: Hawa Koomson elected NPP National Women’s Organiser
items.description: Former Awutu Senya East Member of Parliament Mavis Hawa Koomson has been elected National Women’s Organiser of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), defeating her sole contender, Hajia Safia Mohammed. Madam Koomson secured the position at the party’s National Delegates Conference held at the Baba Yara Sports Stadium in Kumasi on Saturday, October 3, 2026, as more than 7,000 delegates voted to elect a new team of national executives. Her election places her at the helm of the NPP’s women’s wing, with responsibility for coordinating women’s groups across the party’s structures and supporting efforts to strengthen their participation in the party’s activities ahead of the 2028 general election. The contest formed part of a broader exercise to constitute a new national leadership team for the NPP, with delegates also voting in elections for the positions of General Secretary, National Youth Organiser and other national executive portfolios. Justin Frimpong Kodua retained the General Secretary position after polling 4,486 votes. Former Ngleshie Amanfro MP Sylvester Tetteh came second with 1,340 votes, followed by Eugene Boakye Antwi with 162 votes and Dr Charles Dwamena with 126 votes. In the National Youth Organiser contest, Abanga Fuseini Yakubu emerged winner with 1,550 votes. Clement Opoku Gyamfi placed second with 631 votes, while Michael Osei Boateng polled 78 votes. Chris Lloyd Nii Kwei Asamoah, then Deputy National Youth Organiser, secured 46 votes, with Vera Oye Bram-Larbi receiving 44 votes and Alfred Kumi Ababio obtaining 25 votes. The newly elected executives are expected to work together to oversee the NPP’s national operations, strengthen its organisational structures and coordinate preparations for the party’s activities ahead of the 2028 general election.

items.title: John Boadu begins NPP rebuild from grassroots ahead of 2028 election
items.description: Newly elected National Chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), John Boadu, has pledged to begin rebuilding the party from the grassroots as he leads the party towards the 2028 general election. Mr Boadu, speaking after his election at the party’s National Delegates Conference in Kumasi, said the immediate task was to strengthen the NPP’s structures and restore its organisational strength. “Strong parties are not sustained by past achievements alone; they endure because they learn, renew themselves, and respond courageously to a changing society,” he said. He said his administration would build a renewed NPP that listens more, consults more and organises better. “Our task is to build a renewed NPP, one that listens more, consults more, organises better, and prepares more deliberately for the future,” he stated. Mr Boadu said the rebuilding effort would involve regional and constituency executives, external branches, Members of Parliament, patrons and other organised groups within the party. He also pledged to deepen the party’s relationship with voluntary groups, TESCON members, social media practitioners and the traditional media. “A modern political organisation must engage every means of communicating responsibility,” he said. The new chairman placed particular emphasis on young people, saying they must see the NPP as their home. “Our young people must feel that the NPP is their home,” he said. He also promised greater attention to tertiary institutions as centres for political dialogue and leadership development. Mr Boadu said the party would work with its flagbearer and national leadership to strengthen its organisational and financial foundation, particularly at the constituency level. He also called for stronger engagement with the business community and Ghanaian entrepreneurs to promote opportunities and enterprise. But he cautioned that electoral success could not be taken for granted. “Political victory is never an entitlement. It must be earned through service, organisation, credibility, and the trust of the Ghanaian people,” he said. “That is why our preparation begins now.” Mr Boadu said the NPP must rebuild “from the grassroots upwards” by strengthening constituency structures, empowering the youth, supporting women, valuing professionals and listening to traditional and religious leaders. He also called for the party to embrace technology while maintaining the personal relationships that have sustained it. “So I make this commitment: we will serve the New Patriotic Party with humility, lead through consultation, work with every part of our party, and dedicate this mandate to restoring the winning machinery of our great party,” he said. Mr Boadu urged party members to choose “unity over division, service over personal ambition, organisation over disorder, and hope over despair.” He ended by declaring: “JB and his executives are back again. Victory is assured in the year 2028.”

items.title: Titus Glover wins NPP National Organiser race on second attempt
items.description: Former Greater Accra Regional Minister Daniel Nii Kwartei Titus Glover has secured the New Patriotic Party’s National Organiser position, succeeding on his second attempt after losing his first bid for the influential party office. Mr Glover polled 2,964 votes at the NPP’s National Delegates Conference held at the Baba Yara Sports Stadium in Kumasi on Saturday, October 3, 2026, to emerge ahead of six other candidates in the contest. Ali Maiga Halidu placed second with 2,231 votes, while Kwame Prempeh Esq. obtained 445 votes. Korsi Borja polled 145 votes, Seth Agyei Yeboah secured 137, Agyenim Boateng received 105, and Archibald Korletey Gamor obtained 85 votes. The result marks a significant breakthrough for Mr Glover, who had previously contested the National Organiser position but failed to secure the mandate. His return to the race and eventual victory now places him in charge of one of the NPP’s key organisational portfolios. As National Organiser, Mr Glover will be responsible for coordinating the party’s organisational activities and working with its regional, constituency and grassroots structures. The position is central to mobilisation, membership engagement and the coordination of party activities across the country. His election comes as the NPP begins a new phase of internal organisation following its National Delegates Conference. The party is expected to focus on strengthening its structures and mobilising its members ahead of the 2028 general election. Mr Glover will work alongside the newly elected national executives, including National Chairman John Boadu and General Secretary Justin Frimpong Kodua, as the party moves beyond the internal elections and begins preparations for the next electoral cycle.

items.title: Winning 2028 election won’t be easy; we must work harder – Bawumia
items.description: New Patriotic Party (NPP) flagbearer Dr Mahamudu Bawumia has cautioned the party against taking the 2028 general election for granted, stressing that victory will require sustained effort, unity and stronger organisation. Addressing party members and aspirants following the NPP’s national executive elections, Dr Bawumia said the party must recognise the scale of the task ahead and begin working towards the next election with determination. “Winning the 2028 election won’t be easy; we must work harder,” he said, urging members to remain focused and committed to the party’s work beyond the internal elections. Dr Bawumia said the national executive elections should therefore be seen as the start of another phase of mobilisation rather than the end of the party’s internal activities. He encouraged the newly elected executives and other aspirants to combine their strengths and work together to improve the party’s structures. The former Vice President also assured unsuccessful aspirants that they would have roles to play in the party’s preparations for 2028. “You’ll be part of the 2028 campaign. There’s enough work for all of us,” he told them, emphasising the need for the party to draw on the experience and ideas of everyone who participated in the internal contest. The former Vice President’s message comes amid calls by the party’s new National Chairman, John Boadu, for unity following the elections. Mr Boadu has urged members to choose unity over division and described the new mandate as a responsibility that requires the party’s collective effort. Dr Bawumia said the NPP would need to move beyond the competition that characterised the national executive elections and concentrate on strengthening its organisation and reconnecting with its wider membership. He said every member had a role to play in the work ahead. With a new national executive now in place, the party is expected to begin the next phase of its internal organisation and preparations for the 2028 election. Dr Bawumia’s warning emphasises sustained mobilisation and hard work as the NPP seeks to build towards the next national contest.

Addressing the aspirants after the elections, Dr Bawumia said the New Patriotic Party would need the experience, ideas and commitment of all the candidates as it begins preparations for the 2028 general election. “You’ll be part of the 2028 campaign. The aspirants campaigned for different positions and presented their ideas on how they believed the party could strengthen its structures and improve its fortunes. Dr Bawumia said those ideas and experiences could still be useful to the NPP as it begins the next phase of its political organisation. The former Vice President’s message also reinforces calls for unity following the elections, with the new national leadership expected to work with unsuccessful aspirants rather than allowing the internal contests to create divisions within the party. The new executives are expected to work with the party’s grassroots structures as preparations begin for the next general election. Dr Bawumia’s appeal comes as the NPP transitions from its internal elections to the wider task of organising its members and supporters. He said the party would require contributions from all sides, suggesting that the experience gained during the executive contests could be channelled into the party’s broader political activities leading to 2028.

items.title: Today is not a day of victory but a day of responsibility and great unity – John Boadu
items.description: Newly elected National Chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), John Boadu, has urged the party’s new leadership to approach their mandate with a strong sense of responsibility, humility and unity. Speaking after his election at the party’s National Delegates Conference in Kumasi, Mr Boadu said his victory should not be viewed simply as a personal or factional triumph but as the beginning of a collective responsibility to strengthen the NPP. “Today is not a day of victory but a day of responsibility and great unity,” he said, stressing the need for the party to remain focused on its broader objectives rather than allowing the election outcome to create divisions. Mr Boadu’s remarks come after delegates elected a new team of national executives to steer the party’s affairs. The new leadership is expected to work together to coordinate the party’s national, regional and constituency structures while addressing issues that emerged during the campaign for the various executive positions. He said the mandate given to the new executives should serve as a reminder that their positions come with expectations from party members and supporters across the country. He called for a leadership style that places the party’s interests above individual ambitions and encourages cooperation among members. The newly elected chairman also emphasised the importance of unity as the party moves beyond the internal elections. He said the NPP would require the collective efforts of its members, particularly at the grassroots, to strengthen its structures and build a more cohesive organisation. Mr Boadu is expected to work with the newly elected General Secretary Justin Frimpong Kodua, the three Vice Chairmen and other national executives as the party begins a new phase of internal organisation. His message effectively shifts the focus from the contest that brought the new executives into office to the work required after the elections, with unity and collective responsibility forming a central part of his appeal to the party.

Let us choose unity over division – John Boadu to NPP
items.description: Newly elected National Chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), John Boadu, has called on members to put aside internal differences and work towards greater unity following the party’s national executive elections. Mr Boadu said the NPP’s strength would depend on its ability to bring together members with different views, experiences and political backgrounds, rather than allowing disagreements from the election period to create lasting divisions. “Let us choose unity over division,” he told party members, stressing that the completion of the internal elections should mark the beginning of a new phase of collective work. He said the new national executives had a responsibility to serve the entire party and not only the delegates and supporters who backed their respective campaigns. He urged members who contested the various positions, including those who were unsuccessful, to continue contributing to the party’s affairs. Mr Boadu has repeatedly emphasised inclusiveness in his post-election message, telling fellow aspirants that their ideas and experience remain valuable to the NPP. He said the party should harness those contributions as it works to strengthen its structures. He also described the outcome of the elections as a responsibility rather than simply a victory, saying: “Today is not a day of victory but a day of responsibility and great unity.” The National Chairman said the party must now move beyond the competition that characterised the elections and focus on building what he has described as a renewed NPP. He said unity would be essential to that process, particularly as the new leadership begins engaging the party’s structures across the country. The call comes after delegates elected a new team of national executives at the NPP’s National Delegates Conference in Kumasi. The new leadership includes Justin Frimpong Kodua as General Secretary, Kojo Fosu Boadu as First Vice Chairman, Henry Nana Boakye as Second Vice Chairman and Nana Akomea as Third Vice Chairman. Mr Boadu urged the new executives, unsuccessful aspirants and the wider party membership to see themselves as part of one organisation with a shared responsibility. He said the differences that emerged during the contests should not be allowed to overshadow the broader task of strengthening the NPP.

items.title: Burglars steal antiques belonging to Nawab of Bahawalpur’s family in Islamabad
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Robbers and burglars stole cash and valuables worth over Rs34 million in eight incidents in the capital, police said. In the first incident, burglars stole priceless heirlooms and antiques belonging to the family of the Nawab of Bahawalpur, worth Rs20 million, from the house of Prince Bahawal Abbas Khan Abbasi, son of Nawab Salahuddin Abbasi, in F-8/3. Police registered a case under Sections 454 and 380 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC). The incident came to light when the family found the storeroom broken into and the heirlooms and antiques missing. The stolen items included silver and gold articles, including a silver throne chair, silver ladder, silver bowls, silver statues, gold plates, Bahawalpur-crested gold plates and a large crested silver frame bearing the Bahawalpur State crest. Antique arms and heritage weapons, including old musket guns and swords of the Bahawalpur State, were also found missing, along with other valuable articles. The complainant told police that stock-taking and inventory were in progress and that a supplementary list of other missing items would be submitted once the inventory was completed. In the second incident, a gang of robbers looted cash and gold worth Rs3 million from the house of Ali Akbar Naqvi in Naval Anchorage. Four armed men raided the house and held Naqvi’s parents hostage at gunpoint. They then ransacked the house and took eight tolas of gold, a dozen silver rings, two watches, Rs100,000 in cash and other items before escaping. In another incident, a man allegedly looted cash and gold worth Rs2.3 million from a house in Margalla Town. The suspect entered Ali Ashgar’s house by impersonating someone and allegedly threatened the family with dire consequences. Meanwhile, a gang of robbers allegedly snatched a motorcycle from a man in Abbasiabad. Two armed men intercepted Safi Ullah and held him at gunpoint before taking his motorcycle, mobile phone and Rs300,000 in cash. Likewise, burglars stole cash and gold worth over Rs4.4 million from the house of Mohammad Bilal in D-12. The incident took place when the residents had gone to Murree. On their return, they found the house ransacked. Similarly, burglars stole cash and gold from the house of Wasim Ikhlas in Alipur. Moreover, burglars stole cash and valuables worth over Rs4.5 million from the house of Nabil Shahzad in Sri Saral. In another incident, thieves allegedly stole 28 iPhones worth Rs8 million from the house of Ammar Farooq in DHA Phase II. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

items.title: Ireland news conference before Israel game cut short amid tensions
items.description: BACKA TOPOLA: The Republic of Ireland’s press conference on Saturday on the eve of their second Nations League match against Israel in Serbia was cut short as head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions from Israeli journalists. Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in Hungary in their first match on Tuesday following a turbulent build-up in which the Irish squad voted to fulfil the fixture despite unease amongst the team over the war in Gaza. During that match the Irish players wore armbands and pointedly lowered their heads while the Israeli national anthem played. There were no handshakes between the captains before kickoff. With the return leg taking place on Sunday in Backa Topola after the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) refused to host the match at home for security reasons, it was the Ireland manager’s pre-match press conference that gave rise to new tensions. One journalist questioned Hallgrimsson on his thoughts about the incident on Wednesday during a Flydubai flight from the UAE to Israel, which Emirati judicial authorities and Israeli officials have described as a “terrorist act”. “What do you say about the people that you support? Their ideology is based on murder,” one journalist asked. “Just this week, one of them tried to kill 170 Israeli passengers, including 27 innocent children and thousands of others.” An Irish press officer replied: “We are not doing any questions like this today. We are doing football questions.” Another journalist then addressed the Ireland manager: “Your players call our players monkeys during the match…”, only to be immediately interrupted by an FAI official repeatedly insisting “that is completely untrue,” while the microphone was taken away from the reporter in question. “Don’t touch me, don’t touch me,” the journalist exclaimed, as the Irish delegation brought the press conference to an abrupt end. ‘A lot of emotions’ Israeli authorities have condemned the actions taken by the Irish team, with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar accusing Dublin of being on “the wrong side of history.” “Surviving this, coming out of it together as one would be a massive win for me. That is coming from my heart,” Hallgrimsson told journalists. “All the challenges that this team has gone through, all the criticism. “Just surviving as a group after this game, that would be a big win for me and for this group, for the association. “There’s been a lot of emotions from the people in Ireland about this, and obviously that affects the players as well. “We want to do good, but it’s always going to be a challenge when the environment is as noisy as it is. So we try to focus on the football side, and we’ve done a lot of things to help in that area. “One change that we’ve done in the last games is before we go onto the pitch, we do a little prayer and a huddle with the players and all the staff, just to cool our heads before we go onto the pitch. “Conor Coventry has taken that part, so he is now called Brother Coventry in the squad. But it’s really good when you go into a high-intensity and big-pressure game like we’ve been doing, to start the game with cool heads.” Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

items.title: Le Brésil, dernier rempart contre Trump en Amérique du Sud ?
items.description: Aujourd’hui, dimanche 4 octobre, se tiennent les élections présidentielles et législatives brésiliennes , dans un contexte géopolitique particulièrement tendu. Lula avait remporté l'élection présidentielle de justesse en 2022 contre le président sortant Jair Bolsonaro. Son mandat a été particulièrement mouvementé. Le 8 janvier 2023, une semaine après son investiture, une tentative de coup d'État des partisans de Bolsonaro, échoue à Brasília. En septembre 2025, Jair Bolsonaro a été condamné à 27 ans et 3 mois de prison (il est aujourd’hui assigné à résidence) et son fils aîné, Flávio, a été désigné pour lui succéder. Le retour de Trump au pouvoir a d'ailleurs relancé l'extrême droite brésilienne et, depuis 2025, les relations entre les deux présidents oscillent entre pressions trumpistes, notamment sur le commerce, et accalmies temporaires. La gauche a également beaucoup reculé dans la région depuis 2022, et le Brésil fait partie des derniers pays dirigés par un gouvernement progressiste. Il s’agit d’un élément clef de l’élection d’aujourd’hui. Durant la campagne, Lula a continué de défendre les sujets qui l'ont déjà mené au pouvoir : le développement économique, la lutte contre la faim, la pauvreté et la déforestation, avec une volonté affichée de mener une politique étrangère indépendante, souveraine. À l’opposé, Flávio Bolsonaro reprend pour sa part les thématiques chères à son père et à son camp, telles que la lutte contre la criminalité et la corruption, ainsi que la libéralisation de l'économie. Il prône l'alignement sur les États-Unis de Donald Trump et s'appuie principalement sur le vote évangélique. Un élément clef distingue toutefois ce cycle électoral de l'élection présidentielle de 2022 : l'importance accordée à la politique étrangère, qui était quasiment absente lors des précédents scrutins. Ainsi, le 25 juillet, Flávio Bolsonaro avait lancé sa campagne en présence du président argentin Javier Milei, puis avait diffusé un message vidéo du Premier ministre israélien, Benyamin Netanyahou. Flávio Bolsonaro bénéficie également du soutien de Donald Trump, tout comme son frère Eduardo, particulièrement bien introduit dans la sphère MAGA depuis 2018. Condamné pour entrave à la procédure judiciaire, Eduardo Bolsonaro vit aux États-Unis depuis 2025 où il a obtenu une résidence permanente. Il influence directement les différentes décisions de la présidence Trump à l'encontre du Brésil, comme la mise en place de droits de douane. Le 28 mai, les États-Unis ont désigné les deux principaux cartels de narcotrafic brésiliens, le Comando Vermelho et le Primeiro Comando da Capital, comme des organisations terroristes. Selon plusieurs observateurs, cette décision laisse planer le doute sur une intervention équivalente à celle qui s'est produite au Venezuela en cas de victoire de Lula. Ces décisions ont conduit Brasília à une extrême prudence vis-à-vis de Washington, comme en témoigne le refus de délivrer des visas à Riley Barnes et Samuel Samson, deux diplomates américains qui devaient rencontrer plusieurs officiels brésiliens au mois de juillet 2026. Selon le Brésil, cette visite visait à remettre en question le système électoral. Ces dernières semaines, les soupçons d’ingérence américaine dans la campagne présidentielle se sont amplifiés. Le 30 septembre, les médias brésiliens ont révélé que l’ABIN (les services de renseignement brésiliens) avait informé une délégation franco-allemande en visite sur place que les États-Unis et la Russie tentaient d'interférer dans les élections brésiliennes. Le 24 septembre, le Parti des travailleurs de Lula a indiqué que Meta avait bloqué le compte Facebook de Lula et empêché les comptes de campagne du parti de diffuser du contenu politique. Selon Meta, cette mesure serait due à la violation des règles de ces plateformes par les comptes concernés. Comme lors du scrutin de 2022, les résultats devraient être extrêmement serrés entre les deux favoris. Le dernier sondage publié par Datafolha donne Lula à 40 % au premier tour, contre 36 % pour Flávio Bolsonaro. Flávio Bolsonaro semble avoir créé une dynamique positive et a de réelles chances de remporter le scrutin au deuxième tour, surtout si celui-ci se transforme en référendum anti-Lula. Le chiffre à surveiller ce dimanche est l'écart entre Lula et Flávio. Une avance de 5 points ou plus pour Lula lui donnerait de chances de l’emporter, tandis qu'une avance de 3 points ou moins ferait pencher la balance en faveur de Flávio pour le second tour. L’article Le Brésil, dernier rempart contre Trump en Amérique du Sud ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Railways to outsource 13 passenger trains by December
items.description: LAHORE: The Pakistan Railways (PR) has decided to outsource 13 express passenger trains, including Pak Business, and directed its officers to complete the process by December this year. The department has also accelerated efforts to make all faulty (dummy) wagons fit for operation while taking action against the vendors who failed to supply parts on time. “It is the vision of the prime minister as well as mine to make all-out efforts to maintain the railway infrastructure for safe train operation. This is why I have assigned the officers concerned the task to accomplish the target of making all dummy coaches and wagons fit for operation,” Minister for Railways Hanif Abbasi explained while talking to Dawn . “I have also asked the officers to replace the faulty brake cylinders, blocks and shoes with new ones,” he added. According to the minister, the outsourcing of trains and luggage vans is also underway and 13 express passenger trains would be outsourced till Dec 31. For this, the process, including the advertisement and award of the contract, would be completed soon. “At present, the commercial operation of six trains is being carried out by the private parties,” Mr Abbasi said, adding that the trains to be outsourced by December included Sandal, Allama Iqbal Express, Faiz Ahmad Faiz, Fareed Express, Sukkur Express, Babu Passenger, Bulleh Shah Passenger, Mohenjodaro Express, Lasani Express, Sialkot Express, Karachi Express, Bahauddin Zakariya Express and Tezgam. To a question, he said the railway bridge affected by the recent floods on Lahore-Faisalabad track would be rehabilitated within the next two months, helping railways to restore the rail traffic. For the first time, according to him, the freight revenue exceeded the passenger revenue in the railways. “I think, the railways would be able to earn revenue of Rs120bn from the passenger and freight train operations alone by the end of the ongoing fiscal year on June 30,” he hoped. Meanwhile, the minister presided over a meeting at the railway headquarters and directed the authorities to blacklist private vendors responsible for delays in the supply of equipment and materials. During the meeting, matters pertaining to railway operations, revenue generation, maintenance, security and outsourcing came under discussion. Mr Abbasi directed the authorities to install modern CCTV cameras and deploy private security personnel at all railway workshops and yards to prevent theft. He said collective efforts were required to achieve the revenue targets set for the current financial year, adding that locomotives undergoing repairs should be restored to service according to the prescribed schedule. The minister ordered legal action against negligent officials. The meeting was also told by the officers concerned that advance planning was essential for ensuring transparency and improving the railway system. He further directed that the ongoing track renewal work in Sukkur division should be completed by Dec 31 as it would save operational time by around one-and-a-half hours. He also ordered that the flood-damaged Mian Kallar Bridge be completed within 60 days and repair of employees’ residential quarters in Lahore within two months. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

items.title: The court that could not see
items.description: WITNESSES testified that a senior banker sketched private parts on the glass of his desk, asked a woman colleague to name them, and threatened to tear off her clothes if she wore a particular outfit again. Another officer made indecent remarks about her attire before colleagues. The ombudsperson found the charges proved; the Islamabad High Court agreed. On Sept 16, the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) set that judgement aside without substantively engaging with this evidence or the high court’s careful appraisal of it. Its central reason was a definition. Harassment under the 2010 workplace harassment law, it declared, “is only restricted to conduct which is sexual in nature”. Even by that narrow test, the conduct proved was plainly sexual. Before the high court, the officers never contended it fell short of harassment. Why does the FCC confine harassment to sex? The Act’s title and preamble speak of ‘harassment’, not ‘sexual harassment’, and anchor it in the right to dignity. Nor does ‘sexual’ mean only the act of sex; it also means relating to the sexes, or to gender. The Supreme Court said so on review in Nadia Naz, through Justice Ayesha Malik; “sexually demeaning attitudes” means demeaning a person because of their sex. Yale’s Vicki Schultz has shown that much workplace harassment has nothing to do with desire; it belittles women and signals they do not belong. And the 2022 amendment , ignored altogether, covers gender discrimination “which may or may not be sexual in nature”. Courts elsewhere agree. The US supreme court held in Oncale that harassment need not be motivated by desire; Canada and India root it in equality and dignity. India’s law lists “sexually coloured remarks”, exactly what was proved, and the 2021 Nadia Naz judgement the FCC relies on quoted that very provision. ILO Convention 190 treats gender-based harassment, including sexual harassment, as one wrong. This is where a constitutional court should begin. Article 14 declares the dignity of man inviolable, and the Act’s own preamble rests on it. A constitutional court’s first duty is to read statutes through fundamental rights and expand their frontiers, not shrink them. A woman made to name drawings of private parts before her colleagues has had her dignity violated by any measure. Constitutional courts are judged not by the powers they claim but by the rights they protect. Our Supreme Court had already arrived there. In Uzma Naveed (2022) and Muhammad Din (2025), both of which I authored, it held that harassment is not confined to the act of sex and that dignity is absolute and non-negotiable. The FCC dismisses Muhammad Din in one sentence, “with due respect”, ignores Uzma Naveed, and leans instead on the 2021 Nadia Naz judgement the Supreme Court set aside on review. In Haji Adam, decided by the same author the same day, substantial passages reappear word for word; it even names the bank case’s witnesses as the Pemra complainant’s. That raises a serious question whether each record received independent judicial consideration. Precedent is not a courtesy; it is law. Judgements of the Supreme Court delivered before the 27th Amendment bound every court under Article 189. The amendment operates prospectively: it makes the FCC’s decisions binding from now on, but it does not erase nearly eight decades of constitutional jurisprudence. Having inherited the Supreme Court’s constitutional jurisdiction, the FCC inherited the law declared under it. If it doubts that law, the doctrine of precedent requires reasoned reconsideration by a larger bench, not a three-member bench’s single sentence. Even the FCC’s own test, set this March, forbids precedent being “ignored and disregarded in silence”. The deeper problem is the court itself. It was created by the 27th Amendment, rushed through a parliament whose own mandate remains clouded by the disputed elections of February 2024, and carved out of a functioning Supreme Court for reasons never convincingly explained. Britain, the US, India, Canada and Australia entrust constitutional questions to a single apex court, and for good reason: splitting the apex invites conflict and political engineering. South Africa moved the other way in 2013, making its constitutional court the apex court in all matters. Its first bench was chosen by the president on the prime minister’s advice, bypassing the Judicial Commission, with no published criteria or open assessment of merit. Such a court must earn confidence through its work. A judgement rendered without hearing the attorney general or appointing an amicus (even the high court had one), and thin on scholarship and constitutional understanding, does not earn it. Nor does the price: salaries above the Supreme Court’s until that court was raised to match, generous staff allowances, and three more years of tenure. Not a single woman sits on the FCC, a conspicuous absence in a harassment case. I cast no aspersion on any judge who accepted appointment; that is for each conscience. Yet the absence speaks. The women of our judiciary stand apart from this court and deserve the country’s admiration. Such judgements belong to the bar too, for it is very much part of this new judicial era. Bar associations are guarantor institutions; in 2007 they marched until judges were restored. When the architecture of the 26th and 27th Amendments was assembled, that resistance never came. Too many at the bar’s helm measure ambition by proximity to power rather than fidelity to democracy. That is a deficit of character, not of numbers. When the guardians fall silent, unconstitutionalism rises. Constitutional courts are judged not by the powers they claim but by the rights they protect. If this is the direction of travel, dark years lie ahead for rights. Faiz urged us to speak while our lips are still free. It now falls to the lawyers who remember 2007, the academy and those who refuse to be silenced to keep the lamps lit. The writer is a former senior puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, Professor of Practice at SAHSOL, Lums and currently a Visiting Fellow at Yale University, US. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

items.title: Pakistan’s Russian dilemma
items.description: IT is difficult to imagine a single small gesture reducing decades-old hostility between two archrivals. Yet, such a moment was witnessed recently when Alok Dimri, India’s national coordinator for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, visited Islamabad for a meeting. Talking to the state media, he said he was happy to be in Pakistan. It was a simple statement, but perhaps one that may ease some of the cross-border bitterness. Mr Dimri said this while visiting the National Council of Arts in Islamabad. The heritage, art, and culture that Pakistan and India share have repeatedly fallen victim to toxic narratives designed to provoke hate. Yet the cultural link carries a powerful sense of mutual belonging. It may be premature to read too much into the Indian delegate’s visit or to view his words as evidence of a thaw after last May’s stand-off . Still, the episode offers some hope: if leaders on both sides choose to move forward, the dialogue could quickly regain momentum. However, optimism should be tempered — as should any expectation that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will arrive in Islamabad to attend the SCO summit. If he did, it would be a miracle, and the biggest surprise in decades — even bigger than Rajiv Gandhi’s visit to Islamabad in 1988 to attend the Saarc summit or Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s arrival in Lahore in 1999. Both occasions had generated enormous hope for peace between the two neighbours. What actually followed is a familiar story. Another miracle would be if Russian President Vladimir Putin attended the Islamabad SCO summit next year. Pakistan is more curious about this visit and hopes it may trigger a major shift in its geopolitics and ambitions in Central Asia, while influencing the regional discourse in ways that would irritate India. Pakistan would be keen to enhance its defence cooperation with Russia, but particularly interested in making some progress on the much-discussed railway from Moscow to Islamabad and establishing a freight corridor using existing 7,000-kilometre-long railway networks, with Pakistan linked to Russia through Central Asia and/or Iran. Over the decades, Pakistan, the Central Asian states, and Iran have conceived many transnational projects, and each time with great enthusiasm, yet none has materialised. Afghanistan is always made to bear the burden of the blame because of its complex relationship with Pakistan. Russia is likely to remain cautious about deepening its cooperation with Pakistan. Is it not interesting that the conventional wars fought by India and Pakistan collectively may not have lasted for more than a few weeks, and that Pakistan fought its longest war against the Soviet Union in Afghanistan? Pakistan and the Afghan mujahideen, together with the US, defeated the Russians, which was followed by the dismantling of the Soviet state. The Pakistani leadership still takes pride in that success. Of course, times have changed, and Pakistan is looking to cultivate new economic and defence opportunities. Russia, however, is likely to remain cautious about deepening its cooperation with Pakistan. This is not because of their bitter past, from which both sides have moved on, but because of divergent regional interests, particularly over Afghanistan, and Russia’s deep and long-standing engagement with India. Russian-Indian defence and economic cooperation is not necessarily an obstacle to developing ties with Pakistan. But it does mean that Islamabad cannot be regarded as a preferred partner in that context. The disparity in economic relations is significant: Pakistan’s bilateral trade with Russia is less than half a billion dollars, compared with around $69bn in India-Russia trade. The gap is even more pronounced in defence cooperation. India maintains a high level of military engagement with Russia through multiple military-technical cooperation frameworks, including joint research and development, co-development, co-production, and after-sales support. By contrast, Russia’s defence engagement with Pakistan remains selective and falls well short of a strategic military partnership. At the same time, India’s diversification of its defence partnerships has not significantly weakened its relationship with Russia. Moscow may have reservations about some aspects of New Delhi’s growing defence ties with other countries, but there are no clear signs of a fundamental deterioration in bilateral relations. Russia’s interest in Pakistan is, therefore, largely geopolitical — maintaining engagement with Islamabad allows Moscow to show that its international network of partnerships is broad, while also keeping channels open with Pakistan’s political and security leaders, including those who have close ties with US President Donald Trump. Public diplomacy is a domain through which Russia keeps its support club intact and seeks to enhance it, engaging Pakistani media, academics, opinion-makers, and policymakers through exchange programmes. The SCO is another platform Russia uses more extensively than other partners for public diplomacy. Russia and Pakistan share counterterrorism concerns, but their approaches to Afghanistan differ sharply. Russia has recognised the Taliban regime, but Pakistan is fighting a tough war against terrorism and sees Afghanistan as a source of the war. In geo-economic terms, they have different priorities. Russia wants Afgha­n­istan in the camp of its Central Asian allies. At the same time, Pakistan is a major partner of the US in areas where the interests of the two countries converge in Afghanistan. This irritates not only Russia but also China, which wants the US to stay out of the region in its immediate neighbourhood. The US took two decades to leave Afghanistan, and China does not want to see it coming back. It is not surprising that Indian-Russian relations have had few hiccups over decades. At the same time, Pakistan chose the US as its strategic partner after independence. Still, their relationship has not been smooth. Pakistan’s strategic partnership with China has also been tested recently, triggered by CPEC-related disputes and internal security concerns regarding Chinese nationals in Pakistan. Perhaps Russia is a new love interest for a segment of Pakistan’s power elite, but the two have little to share. And the last optimistic note: what if India and Pakistan decide to live in peace? What would the geopolitical impact be? The writer is a security analyst. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

items.title: Yemen offensive
items.description: IT appears that escalation is on the cards where the Houthi-Saudi and US-Iran conflicts are concerned. As per reports, Riyadh is planning an offensive to help the Yemeni government — which it backs — retake the strategically important Red Sea coast area from the pro-Iran Houthis, who captured it during a lightning offensive last month. Hostilities are continuing; there were reports on Saturday of both Riyadh and Sana’a being attacked . Meanwhile, members of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement are due to hold an emergency meeting to discuss the Yemen situation. Regarding Iran, the US has reportedly ordered thousands more troops, as well as an aircraft carrier group, to the Gulf. This mirrors the build-up of American forces around Iran before the US-Israeli assault targeted the Islamic Republic in late February. Top US officials have reportedly met at Camp David to discuss the Yemen and Iran files. Diplomacy, it seems, is giving way to more war in the Gulf and the wider Middle East. The humanitarian situation in Yemen is dire, with hundreds of thousands of people uprooted, while the UN says millions of Yemenis, including more than 2m infants, face acute hunger. If the Yemen war sucks in more regional states, it will complicate matters further. The best option, therefore, is for Muslim and Arab states to help restore the Saudi-Houthi ceasefire. The Houthi Ansarallah group must pledge to stop its attacks on Saudi Arabia, while ensuring free passage through Bab al-Mandeb. The Saudis, on their part, should consider lifting the blockade of Houthi territory, while encouraging all Yemeni factions to peacefully resolve the internal conflict. The Yemen war has been raging for over a decade, and previous external interventions have failed to end it; in fact, continued violence has exacerbated the humanitarian situation. With regard to Iran, it appears that President Donald Trump’s administration has halted kinetic action only till the November US midterms, and plans to restart hostilities after elections are out of the way. This would be a grave error. US-Israeli aggression has caused great loss of life in Iran as well as damage to infrastructure, while the global economy has been shell-shocked due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The world — particularly the states of the region — cannot afford more disruption and war. Mr Trump has turned down the recent Iranian proposal to open Hormuz. He should reconsider his strategy and restart dialogue with Tehran, while the Iranians should promise to reopen the strait if the US lifts its blockade of Iran and eases sanctions. The US leader has hailed the exit of American troops from Iraq. He should work on a similar plan to bring his forces home from elsewhere in the Gulf and end the Iran war. items.title: Analysis: Why lower inflation still feels expensive
items.description: A SLOWDOWN in inflation may offer some statistical relief to the government, but prices of everyday essentials remain substantially higher than they were two years ago. The apparent contradiction lies in the difference between what inflation measures and what consumers experience when they enter the market. Headline inflation measures how quickly the overall price basket is changing. It does not show how far the general price level has already risen. The official measure is based on prices collected from different markets and cities and combined into urban, rural and national indices. Therefore, a national average may not correspond to the retail price paid by an individual consumer in a particular market. Lower inflation does not mean prices have returned to previous levels. It simply means that they are rising more slowly on average. Consumers continue to bear the cumulative impact of price increases recorded in previous years. This helps explain why easing inflation has yet to translate into a comparable reduction in the cost of living. A comparison of Pakistan Bureau of Statistics prices between October 2024 and October 2026 illustrates the extent of that accumulated burden. Several essential food and energy items remained substantially more expensive than they were two years earlier, even though headline inflation later moderated. Among the sharpest increases were those in onions, electricity, diesel and petrol. Slower inflation masks cumulative rise in essential prices over past two years These individual price movements do not, of course, represent overall inflation, which is calculated from a weighted basket of goods and services. But they help explain the disconnect between official inflation readings and what consumers encounter in retail markets. Wheat flour provides one of the clearest examples. The national average price of a 20kg flour bag increased from Rs1,835 in October 2024 to Rs2,697 in October 2026 — an increase of 47 per cent. Beef with bone became 26.7pc more expensive, while the price of a 2.5kg tin of vegetable ghee rose by 18.5pc. Retail prices in individual markets can be even higher than these national averages. The increases were steeper in transport fuels. Petrol rose from Rs248.18 per litre in October 2024 to Rs389.51 in October 2026, an increase of 56.9pc. High-speed diesel increased from Rs252.43 to Rs402.53 per litre over the same period, a rise of 59.5pc. This is where the distinction between inflation and the price level becomes especially important. Inflation captures the pace at which prices are changing across a weighted basket. By contrast, consumers confront the actual price level when buying flour, meat, fuel and other necessities. Several factors are contributing to the current price pressures, but former economic adviser to the government Dr Ashfaq Hasan Khan attributes them largely to higher global energy prices and domestic food prices, particularly wheat. He said higher energy prices were a global phenomenon, but governments elsewhere had sought to cushion consumers by reducing the incidence of taxation. In Pakistan, he argued, the impact of higher international energy prices had been compounded by the petroleum levy. “The petroleum levy is the root cause of rising inflation in Pakistan, besides higher global energy and food prices,” Dr Khan said, referring to a levy of Rs85 per litre. He described the current pressures as predominantly from the supply side rather than the result of excessive consumer demand. That distinction matters for the choice of policy response, he argued. “IMF is pressurising Pakistan to devalue its exchange rate and also increase SBP policy rate,” he said. Under a conventional IMF stabilisation programme, tighter monetary policy is used to curb demand, helping contain inflation and ease balance-of-payments pressures. But if inflation is being driven mainly by energy costs, petroleum levies and food prices, higher interest rates do not directly address the underlying sources of the increase, Dr Khan argued. “Raising interest rates is not the right solution to supply-side inflation,” he said, referring to the IMF demand for an increase in interest rates. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

items.title: La mayoría del PSOE y el Gobierno anima a Sánchez a convocar elecciones ya: “Ahora hay una oportunidad”
items.description: La gran mayoría de los dirigentes del PSOE y de los miembros socialistas del Gobierno ha llegado a la conclusión de que la mejor opción es adelantar ya las elecciones para el 29 de noviembre , la primera fecha posible. Por eso casi todos los que están hablando con el presidente, Pedro Sánchez, le están animando a hacerlo, según coinciden diversas fuentes. Él continúa con una larga ronda de llamadas que ya empezó el jueves por la tarde, cuando en el núcleo duro empezaron a saber que Junts iba a tumbar los decretos . Ahí ya empezó una larga lista de consultas sobre el posible adelanto electoral, que se intensificó el viernes y siguió el sábado. Como es habitual, Sánchez escucha pero no comparte con nadie su posición, y por tanto siempre puede haber una sorpresa. Con todo, la mayoría de los ministros y dirigentes consultados creen que al final acabará anunciando el lunes la convocatoria. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El posible adelanto electoral fuerza a la izquierda alternativa a acelerar
items.description: Buena parte del espacio a la izquierda del PSOE se echó a temblar el jueves por la noche, cuando Junts anunció que tumbaría los dos decretos de vivienda en el Congreso y por los grupos de Telegram de los partidos comenzó a correr el rumor de que Pedro Sánchez sopesaba un adelanto electoral . Los matices en las declaraciones de los distintos portavoces del grupo la mañana del viernes eran evidentes y no menores, oscilando entre el “estamos preparados” o el “vamos a estarlo”. La realidad es que los partidos de Sumar en el Gobierno (Izquierda Unida, Comuns, Más Madrid y Movimiento Sumar), rebautizados bajo la marca Frente Amplio para las generales, llevan desde febrero sin haber sido capaces de designar al relevo de la vicepresidenta Yolanda Díaz y despejar el resto de incógnitas en torno a su proyecto. Todos coinciden en que se han quedado ya sin margen y que la coyuntura va a precipitar todas las decisiones en los próximos días. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El PP ya especula con un Gobierno Feijóo
items.description: El PP de Alberto Núñez Feijóo hace tiempo que anhela elecciones y le da igual la fecha, según distintas fuentes de su equipo. Creen que esta vez es inviable el gatillazo de julio de 2023 y que a Pedro Sánchez solo le puede ir peor, elija lo que elija. El líder popular transmite en público que está listo, preparado, casi ansioso para exigir la cita con las urnas “cuanto antes”, que va a ser casi el único lema de su programa en estas semanas, pero en privado pide prudencia. En su entorno han empezado a rellenar quinielas. Reconocen que le falta equipo, sobre todo para los grandes Ministerios de Estado, como Exteriores, Defensa o Interior, pero vaticinan que esos huecos se rellenarían con perfiles de los cuerpos de élite en cuanto pueda gobernar. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Junts fía su resurgir al impacto de la vuelta de Puigdemont
items.description: Girona fue la ciudad escogida este sábado para arrancar en Cataluña la primera de las manifestaciones convocadas por el Sindicato de Inquilinas tras el bloqueo de los decretos de vivienda que pretendía aprobar el Gobierno y que paralizaron Junts, PP y Vox. La convocatoria no reunió a más de 700 personas, según la Policía Municipal. Este mismo año, y atendiendo a las cifras publicadas por medios locales, en Girona salió más gente a la calle en movilizaciones por Palestina, el 8-M, o para la celebración del Mundial de fútbol de la selección española. Ninguna de ellas llegó a las 10.000 que aglutinó la Diada. Desde 2017 se han celebrado tres elecciones para elegir presidente de la Generalitat. En Girona, Junts ha sido la fuerza más votada en todas ellas, con más del 30% de los votos. El partido saca idéntica victoria si se toma en cuenta el resultado de toda la provincia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: A Sol no llega el fin del mundo
items.description: Viernes noche en Madrid. Cuando en Preciados se adivinan ya las tiendas de campaña de Sol y los carteles enormes que anuncian la lucha, una voz que no se sabe de dónde viene clama entre las muchedumbres. Pertenece a un hombre desgañitado, viejito de pelo blanco, con la nariz y el mentón casi encontrándose. Se llama Héctor, es ecuatoriano y tiene mérito: al lado de la zona cero de las masivas protestas por una vivienda digna , con España en convulsión harta de precios prohibitivos y desahucios, Héctor predica el fin del mundo y pide a la gente que vuelva a Dios. “¿Qué le parece lo que está ocurriendo ahí, en Sol?”, le pregunta el periodista señalando la plaza. Héctor, escoltado por una mujer llamada Noemí, se acerca y susurra misteriosamente: “Los tiempos finales son siempre tiempos peligrosos. Tiempos inciviles”. Luego, pide a Noemí que enseñe al periodista unos textos de Timoteo. “Lo primero que tiene que hacer la gente es arrepentirse y volver a Dios”, concluye. Y se despide con una sonrisa para volver al vociferío. Seguir leyendo

items.description: Esta es la cuarta entrevista del día para Sylvester Stallone . ¿Cansado ya de hablar tanto? “No, porque esta es la primera sobre mis memorias”, responde en la habitación del hotel de Nueva York, su ciudad natal, frente a Central Park, donde recibe a EL PAÍS. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Un agujero en las últimas 36 horas de la “vida bonita” del arquitecto Juanpere
items.description: En plena crisis de la vivienda por el caso Maricarmen , Pedro Sánchez visitó el lunes una promoción de vivienda protegida en el distrito del Poblenou de Barcelona. Es el único inmueble público existente en esa manzana y su sobrio diseño contrasta con el resto de modernos edificios de oficinas de fachadas desiguales y acristaladas que se levantan sobre los chaflanes. Forman parte de un proyecto impulsado por un fondo de inversión local y sus bocetos, como muchos otros de la ciudad, salieron de las mesas de trabajo de GCA Architects, un exitoso estudio fundado en la ciudad que desde hacía unos días está sumido en la consternación. Lo que apuntaba a la muerte natural el 26 de diciembre de uno de sus fundadores y socios, Josep Juanpere, estalló de forma repentina el 23 de septiembre como un posible homicidio cometido supuestamente por quien era su pareja sentimental, Belén L., miembro de una conocida familia de la jet-set madrileña que fue detenida aquel día y está siendo investigada por el fallecimiento del arquitecto. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La cara oculta del éxito de Starship: Musk deja fuera de juego a la NASA con su plan para dominar el cielo
items.description: Elon Musk pisa el acelerador con su Starship. Su nave estrella, la más grande de la historia, entró por primera vez en órbita este lunes; y su compañía espacial, SpaceX, ya tiene autorización de la administración federal de EE UU para que, si quiere, pueda agilizar la actual fase de pruebas y lanzarla dos veces más en octubre. Y Musk no pretende quedarse ahí: “En dos o tres años, despegará una Starship cada hora”, declaró la semana pasada en su red social X. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Cristina Pardo: “Los políticos son mis empleados, por eso soy una jueza severa con todos”
items.description: Cristina Pardo acude todos los días, todo el día, a la tele donde trabaja hace 20 años, aunque su nuevo programa, La mesa , se emita solo la noche de los miércoles. “Jamás en mi vida he venido a mesa puesta” bromeará luego, jugando con el nombre de su espacio y sus muchos trienios detrás y delante de las cámaras. Así que, para optimizar tiempo y aprovechar el servicio de maquillaje y peluquería para salir bien en la foto, propone charlar en la sede de Atresmedia, donde conviven las redacciones y los platós de La Sexta, su cadena hasta hace nada, y Antena 3, su nueva cabecera . Todo queda en casa. Seguir leyendo GRAMÁTICA 'PARDO' Cristina Pardo (Pamplona, Navarra, 49 años) quiso ser abogada antes de decidirse por el periodismo, por emular a su admirado José María García, al que gustaba de oír aunque no tuviera ni idea de fútbol. La capacidad de atrapar al oyente, o al espectador, que tanto admiraba Pardo de García, ha sido, después, uno de sus propios fuertes. Después de trabajar en radio, dio el salto a la televisión, en La Sexta, donde su particular estilo ante las cámaras como cronista política siguiendo al Partido Popular, le hizo hacerse, casi, una marca en programas como Liarla Pardo y Más vale tarde . Desde esta temporada, presenta La mesa , en Antena 3.

items.title: Ay, nuestro Woody...
items.description: Al viejo clarinetista le regalaron las autoridades madrileñas una guitarra y él la tomó en sus manos, medio aburrido, con esa actitud resignada que muestra ante personas que en otros tiempos hubiéramos considerado absolutamente ajenas al mundo del cineasta. Porque Woody era nuestro, y nosotros, hablo de los de entonces, teníamos a Allen por un tipo de izquierdas, por un progre al estilo europeo, tal y como entendíamos que era eso. Nosotros, aún no contemplábamos que hubiera un nosotras, estábamos convencidos de que sus películas reflejaban la sociedad neoyorquina, la de una clase media intelectual, estilosa y con tiempo y dinero para salir a Elaine’s por las noches. Nosotros, menos aún nosotras, jamás percibíamos que el personaje masculino solía tomar la palabra y no la soltaba, y que solo gracias a que la actriz solía ser una mujer de la talla y la gracia de Diane Keaton lograba hacerse visible e icónica. Nosotros, incluidas nosotras, veíamos también como natural que una chiquilla, casi púber, como Mariel Hemingway se enamorara perdidamente del maduro neurótico , y comprendíamos que llorara por tener que volar sola. Nosotros, los de entonces, creíamos ver un mensaje social donde solo brillaba lo romántico. Nosotros no habríamos soportado que se nos dijera que sus películas entroncaban más con las encantadoras comedias de enredo con las que él había crecido, que con un cine comprometido; por creer, creíamos nosotros que el jazz que ilustraba sus historias era una elección intelectual, y eso que él se encargó de explicarnos que era la música que escuchaba en la radio cuando era chico. Pero nosotros amoldamos el personaje a nuestras necesidades históricas. Queríamos que Woody fuera el hombre a la medida de un país, el nuestro, que estaba abriéndose a la democracia y, a pesar de que nos repetía hasta la saciedad que no era un intelectual, así lo considerábamos. Los admiradores son exigentes y ciegos. Hasta sus películas más hondas respondían a lo sentimental, a las inherentes obsesiones humanas, más que a la relación con la sociedad. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Estudiantes reclutados por Telegram, saboteadores amateur y sicarios: así externaliza Rusia sus operaciones en Europa
items.description: La noche del 20 de marzo de 2024, especialmente húmeda y templada en Londres, tres veinteañeros se plantaron en un polígono industrial del este de la ciudad a bordo de un Kia Picanto rojo cereza. Entraron, prendieron fuego a un almacén y grabaron el incendio con un teléfono móvil. El vídeo de las llamas devorando el local acabó en manos de otro joven de 20 años, Dylan Earl, captado a través de la aplicación de mensajería Telegram por la organización paramilitar rusa Wagner, de la órbita del Kremlin, y que a su vez había reclutado a otros para hacer el trabajo sucio. Una de las naves incendiadas contenía ayuda humanitaria y equipos de satélite Starlink destinados a Ucrania. Según la investigación británica, los tres jóvenes que prendieron la mecha no sabían que trabajaban en realidad para Rusia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Juicio al alcalde que arruinó un pueblo gastando millones de euros en piedras de granito
items.description: En el número 12 de la Ribera de Curtidores, en pleno Rastro madrileño, hay una tienda de “arte y antigüedades” llamada Duino . Es un espacio de aproximadamente 15 metros cuadrados en el que se concentran bustos de piedra, capiteles, cuadros clásicos y modernos llenan las paredes, esculturas clásicas y de diseño con colores chillones se reparten por el habitáculo, globos terráqueos... Al fondo de ese batiburrillo, se encuentra un pequeño mostrador que atiende Eva Mejías, en su día concejala de Cultura de Navalcarnero, un municipio de 33.300 habitantes al suroeste de la capital de España. Junto al mostrador, sentado en una silla, con las piernas cruzadas, su pareja y propietario del negocio: Baltasar Santos, quien fuera durante 20 años —entre 1995 y 2015— alcalde por el PP de esa población madrileña, hasta que le echó del partido Esperanza Aguirre tras conocer que estaba imputado en tres procesos judiciales y que había acumulado 200 millones de euros de deuda en su Ayuntamiento, entre otras cosas, comprando piedras y piezas de granito. “Dejé el pueblo mejor de lo que me lo encontré”, aseguraba sin empacho este viernes Santos a las puertas de su tienda, abierta tras dejar su dilatada actividad municipal y donde también exhibe sus libros de poesía. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Fondos buitre, turistas y alquileres imposibles: ¿qué tipo de ciudad queremos?
items.description: “Madrid / nos pertenece / a ti y a mí”. Aplíquese a Madrid, o a cualquier otra ciudad. Es un verso de Biznaga, la célebre banda de punk rock, conocida por sus letras críticas, siempre atentas a los trances sociopolíticos. El pasado domingo 27 de septiembre, en la acampada por la vivienda en la madrileña Puerta del Sol, se comprobó que es uno de los estribillos que, con los brazos en alto, el público más corea. Hay algo ahí que importa. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ascensión, la isla desértica que se hizo selva
items.description: Casi en el punto exacto en mitad del Atlántico entre África y América del Sur, si trazáramos una línea por debajo del ecuador, existe una isla que hace 200 años estaba deshabitada y era, según un escritor de la época, “la abominación de la desolación”. “Ascensión solo produce tortugas, ratas e insomnio”, dijo otro. “La tierra más desolada y yerma (como una tierra maldita por Dios) que jamás vieron mis ojos… Creo que el mundo entero no ofrece otro pedazo de suelo semejante”, añadió otro más. Ascensión está tan lejos (1.100 kilómetros del lugar más cercano, la isla de Santa Elena; 1.600 del punto más cercano en África, y 2.300 de Brasil) que no llegó ni una sola semilla de ninguna planta hasta que los humanos, británicos en concreto, se asentaron en ella. “No hay tierra, no hay sombras, no hay plantas, no hay agua”, escribió uno de sus primeros habitantes. Y, sin embargo, Ascensión tiene una enorme importancia geoestratégica desde que fue descubierta y, a pesar de esa desolación, o precisamente por ella, ahora tiene un gigantesco valor medioambiental. También pasó por allí otro famosísimo escritor, científico y revolucionario de la biología, Charles Darwin. Gracias a él y a una historia de coraje, cabezonería, biología e ingeniería, esta isla improbable podría contener el secreto de la lucha contra la desertificación en el mundo, y un joven científico español está trabajando para probarlo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El “turno” de Feijóo, cueste lo que cueste
items.description: Los barones del PP decidieron que había llegado el turno de Alberto Núñez Feijóo en la madrugada del 24 de febrero de 2022 , cuando la guerra descarnada de Isabel Díaz Ayuso y Pablo Casado alcanzó un punto de no retorno y todo el PP se puso a mirar a Galicia. Aquella noche negra en la que Rusia invadió Ucrania , los populares depositaron en el mejor de sus presidentes autonómicos, el más ampliamente respetado por el resto, el liderazgo de un PP en permanente cuenta atrás para el desalojo de Pedro Sánchez de La Moncloa. ¿Habría cogido el tren a Madrid el entonces presidente de la Xunta si le cuentan que tendría que estar al menos una legislatura en la oposición? La respuesta hoy solo es política ficción pero, por aquel entonces, ni en las peores pesadillas se manejaba como hipótesis que Sánchez pudiera mantenerse en el poder hasta ahora. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Thomas Piketty: “El futuro que nos están preparando los multimillonarios es distópico”
items.description: La mayor parte del planeta con ingresos equivalentes a 5.000 euros al mes en el año 2100. Las temperaturas promedio, solo 1,8 grados por encima de las de la era preindustrial. Menos carne, industria y minería. Más salud y educación. ¿Y los perjudicados? Los Jeff Bezos, Larry Ellison y Elon Musk del mundo. Un reducidísimo grupo de ricos que representan el 0,001% de la población y pasaría de concentrar el actual 6,4% del patrimonio mundial al 0,05%, mientras que el 50% más pobre del planeta pasaría de tener solo un 2% para llegar al 30%. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Brasil decide su futuro entre Lula y Bolsonaro, un estadista desgastado y el hijo de un ultra
items.description: Brasil celebra este domingo unas elecciones presidenciales y legislativas que son el tercer duelo electoral consecutivo entre la izquierda democrática que representa Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva y la extrema derecha de los Bolsonaro. Cambian los protagonistas pero no la sustancia. Lula, de 80 años, proclama que el pueblo está llamado “a elegir entre democracia y barbarie”; el senador Flávio Bolsonaro , de 45, eleva la batalla a confrontación “entre el Bien contra el Mal”. Los comicios son un mano a mano entre un estadista desgastado que busca un cuarto mandato, y el heredero político, investigado por corrupción, de un movimiento político ultra. Un aspirante al que se adhieren conservadores y todo el que odia a Lula . El ambiente es de apatía aunque los favoritos llevan meses empatados en las encuestas, proponen modelos antagónicos de país y, literalmente, no quedan casi indecisos. Es muy improbable, pero no imposible, que la elección presidencial quede decidida esta noche. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El apocalipsis laboral de la IA se pospone (por ahora)
items.description: Hay tres versiones del Apocalipsis de San Juan, un texto que nunca pierde vigencia, anticipando los impactos de la inteligencia artificial (IA). Una: la reciente y aterradora perspectiva de la muerte descendiendo de enjambres de máquinas autónomas asesinas impulsadas por la IA , en un trasunto del 2001 de Stanley Kubrik. Dos: un sector cuyas expectativas imposibles está hinchando la madre de todas las burbujas financieras hasta niveles que ríete tú de la Gran Recesión y sus uvas de la ira. Y tres: el fin del trabajo, la reconversión brutal y, a lo peor, la desaparición de millones de empleos , empezando por primera vez en la historia por los de la gente más formada, que puede llevar a la economía global camino de una depresión, a niveles de desigualdad imposibles y a una mezcla de tecnofatalismo, resentimiento y rabia (algo que ya sucede, dicho así entre paréntesis, pero elevado a la enésima potencia). Las utopías y las distopías son máquinas de novelar. Escupen titulares con pegada, latigazos líricos plagados de esdrújulas finiseculares y de sílabas hinchadas como nubes de tormenta. Pero a menudo impiden ver lo que de veras está pasando: que esas visiones hiperbólicas son interesadas. La mayor parte de esos miedos los están inoculando las propias empresas o los gobernantes que las protegen, pensando en su poder y en su cuenta de resultados. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Tight monetary policy likely to continue
items.description: KARACHI: As the world continues to grapple with uncertain oil prices, the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) is unlikely to meet its FY27 mid-term inflation target of 5-7 per cent, financial experts and analysts said. Consumer Price Index-based inflation of 10.3 per cent in September clearly indicates that industry, businesses, and the general public will bear the brunt of these cost-push inflationary pressures. Experts believe the central bank will not lower interest rates to stimulate economic activity. Instead, it will maintain a tight monetary stance to support ‘sustainable’ growth. For the past four years, the government and the SBP have been satisfied with low but sustainable growth of around 3 to 3.7 per cent—a level that creates no jobs and does not address the severe problem of 44 per cent of Pakistanis living in poverty. “There is no domestic or foreign investment, and existing industries are struggling to survive. The situation would not change unless a comprehensive economic policy is introduced to support domestic investment, which is being undermined by inflated energy prices and overall double-digit inflation,” said Amir Aziz, a manufacturer and exporter of textile made-ups. “Inflation is only one factor. Bangladesh is in a much better position, as energy costs about 7 to 8 cents per unit, compared with 14 to 16 cents in Pakistan. This gives Bangladesh an advantage over Pakistani products,” said Mr Mohammad Hasham, who recently returned home after serving the Bangladesh textile industry for 25 years as the head of some of its largest textile units. He said double-digit inflation is killing both the industry and investors, and economic activity is slowing, causing pain for the general public. Tresmark Chief Executive Faisal Mamsa said that Pakistan’s authorities reportedly expect inflation to average around 7.5pc if oil returns towards $80, and around 8.2pc if it remains near $100 per barrel. “They also expect inflation to moderate after December and argue that the current 11.5pc policy rate remains appropriate,” he said. However, many experts disagree that the SBP policy rate will remain unchanged at 11.5pc despite double-digit inflation. At the same time, the government raised cut-off yields by up to 75 basis points, with the highest at 12.49pc for the one-year tenor at Wednesday’s T-bill auction. The hike in returns on risk-free government papers reflected a possible rise in the SBP policy rate at the next Monetary Policy Committee meeting on Oct 26. Mr Mamsa said the stable rupee helps contain imported inflation. Higher domestic fuel prices allow demand and imports to adjust. “The IMF, meanwhile, continues to emphasise a more market-based exchange rate. The authorities are reluctant to reopen the imported inflation Pandora’s Box,” he said, adding that a market-based exchange rate parity does not automatically mean a weaker rupee. “If remittances remain strong, reserves continue improving, the current account stays manageable, and the dollar demand remains contained, price discovery can still produce a stable currency,” he said. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

items.title: FAO flags gaps in Pakistan’s nutritious food supply
items.description: • UN agency says over 60pc of citizens unable to afford healthy diet • Calls for overhaul of agrifood system ISLAMABAD: The Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) of the United Nations has emphasised the urgent need to transform Pakistan’s agrifood system to improve access to healthy diets, a critical step towards addressing all forms of malnutrition and their related costs to society. The UN agency, in its latest assessment on “Food Supply for Healthy Diets in Pakistan”, observed that a major challenge in the country’s current food supply is the persistent mismatch between the quantities of food available and those required for the population to consume a healthy diet aligned with the national food-based dietary guidelines (FBDGs). “Enabling access to healthy diets for all is essential to achieving Pakistan’s national development priorities. Yet over 60 per cent of Pakistanis cannot afford a healthy diet, contributing to the high rates of malnutrition across the country. At the same time, diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCD) are rising, while various forms of undernutrition persist. Unhealthy diets are a common cause of all forms of malnutrition and contribute directly to morbidity and mortality from NCD,” the assessment shows. The FAO listed priority policy actions to strengthen demand for healthy diets through consumer-focused policies; updating Pakistan’s FBDGs to reflect nutrition, health, and environmental priorities and use it for nutrition education and behavior change; introducing evidence-based fiscal measures, including taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages and other foods high in sugar, salt, and unhealthy fats; introducing front-of-pack nutrition labelling to help consumers make informed food choices; protecting vulnerable populations; restricting the marketing of unhealthy foods, particularly those targeting children, expanding nutritious school meal programmes; and strengthening social protection programmes to improve access to nutritious foods. The assessment recommended reorienting the agrifood system to deliver healthy diets, aligning agricultural policies and investment priorities to increase support for the production of vegetables, fruits, pulses, roots and tubers across the country, while supporting milk production in some regions; and providing greater incentives for food processors to meet food safety and quality standards and reformulate foods to reduce salt, sugar and unhealthy fats. It called for promoting healthier retail food environments, through investments in storage, cold chains, and market infrastructure to reduce losses. These actions, combined with regular monitoring, can contri­bute to increasing access to and consumption of healthy diets in Paki­stan, both today and in the future. The FAO assessment says large gaps were observed for several nutritious food groups, particularly vegetables, roots and tubers, fruits, and legumes and pulses. However, important misalignment exists between Pakistan’s dietary guidelines and food supply, with supply gaps for several nutritious food groups, particularly vegetables, roots and tubers, fruits, legumes and pulses, while the supply for staples and sugar exceeds what is needed for healthy diets. “Enabling equitable access to diverse, nutritious, safe, and affordable foods that support healthy diets is a policy imperative for Pakistan,” the assessment said. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

items.title: Chinese envoy: China urges improved global human rights governance
items.description: China has called on the international community to establish a just, equitable and inclusive global human rights governance system guided by the Global Governance Initiative. Jia Guide, China's permanent representative to the UN Office at Geneva and other international organizations in Switzerland, made the remarks on Wednesday while delivering a joint statement entitled "Improving International Human Rights Governance," on behalf of 71 countries at the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council at the Palais des Nations. The Global Governance Initiative, proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping on September 1, 2025, has received support and positive responses from numerous countries and international organizations. Jia noted in the joint statement that the international landscape is undergoing profound changes amid a complex and turbulent environment, while global human rights governance is facing profound adjustments. He said that China puts forward four proposals: First, adopt a people-centered approach. It is up to the people of each country to assess and improve their own human rights situation, so as to stay true to the original aspiration of human rights governance and meet people's needs. Second, uphold sovereign equality. All countries should participate, make decisions and benefit on an equal footing. Greater attention should be paid to the voices of the Global South. China advocates fairness, objectivity and non-selectivity, and calls for dialogue and cooperation based on mutual respect. Third, uphold fairness and justice. China opposes the politicization and instrumentalization of human rights, takes a holistic approach to all categories of human rights, advances human rights reform in a prudent manner, and supports multilateral human rights institutions and experts in discharging their mandates objectively and impartially. Fourth, uphold the international rule of law. China champions the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, ensures the equal and consistent application of international law and international rules, and opposes double standards, interference in the internal affairs of other countries under the pretext of human rights, and imposition of one's own standards on others. The joint statement is based on the platform of The Group of Friends of Global Governance in Geneva, officially launched on February 27, 2026, at the Palais des Nations.
